children.title: Population Risk Objectives
children.top_down_role: Covers objectives indexed by an underlying population distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Population Risk Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional risk for a possibly nonsmooth loss over a finite-dimensional decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, and let \(\ell:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be measurable in its random argument. The population risk associated with \(P\) is the extended-real function \[R_P(x):=\int_\Xi \ell(x,\xi)\,P(d\xi),\qquad x\in X,\] whenever this integral is well-defined, meaning that the positive and negative parts are not both infinite. A population-risk problem is \(\inf_{x\in X}R_P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A population-risk problem minimizes the distributional average of a loss over the decision set, provided the extended expectation is well-defined.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) is a probability space and \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty.
For every \(x\in X\), the map \(\xi\mapsto\ell(x,\xi)\) is measurable.
The positive and negative expected parts of \(\ell(x,\cdot)\) are not simultaneously infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_P(x)=\int_\Xi\ell(x,\xi)\,P(d\xi)\) defines the population objective on its effective domain.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of population risk

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and fits the population-risk leaf, but no inspectable citation or locator supports it.

children.title: Expectation-Form Objectives
children.top_down_role: Covers expectation-based representations used by stochastic methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-Form Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-integrand representation of an extended-real stochastic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) be a random element with law \(P\), and let \(f(\cdot,\xi):X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a random extended-real function. If \(f(x,\xi)\) is measurable and its expectation is well-defined for every \(x\) in the effective domain, then the expectation-form objective is \[F(x):=\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]=\int_\Xi f(x,z)\,P(dz).\] The associated stochastic optimization problem is \(\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\); nonsmoothness or weak convexity is imposed samplewise or directly on \(F\), not by the expectation notation alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation-form objective is the expected value of a measurable random extended-real function, optimized over a prescribed decision set.
assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), \(f(x,\xi)\) is measurable and has a well-defined expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]\) is an expectation-form objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation representation is correct and appropriately distinguished from weak convexity or nonsmoothness assumptions, but it lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Population-to-Sample Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Covers the structural connection between population criteria and sampled surrogates.

knowledge_statements.title: Population-to-Sample Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical approximation obtained by replacing the population law with an empirical measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\) be observations in \(\Xi\), and define the empirical measure \(P_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\xi_i}\). For every \(x\in X\) at which the displayed quantities are defined, replacing \(P\) by \(P_n\) gives \[R_{P_n}(x)=\int_\Xi \ell(x,\xi)\,P_n(d\xi)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x,\xi_i).\] Thus the empirical finite-sum objective is the plug-in counterpart of the population risk; equality with \(R_P\) is not asserted for finite \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substituting the empirical distribution for the population law converts a population expectation into the sample-average finite sum.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\ell(x,\xi_i)\) is defined for the considered \(x\in X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical-measure substitution identity is correct and fits the correspondence leaf, but no supporting citation with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Empirical Risk Objectives
children.top_down_role: Covers data-indexed objectives formed from observed samples.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Risk Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted sample-average risk based on a fixed observed dataset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\) and sample loss \(\ell:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the empirical risk is \[R_n(x):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x,\xi_i),\qquad x\in X,\] with the extended-real sum interpreted only where it is unambiguous. Empirical risk minimization seeks any \(\widehat x_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}R_n(x)\), when this set is nonempty; otherwise the problem is expressed through its infimum or approximate minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical risk is the average loss on a fixed dataset; empirical risk minimization minimizes that finite-sample average.
assumptions_latex: The finite extended-real sum is unambiguous on the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x,\xi_i)\) is the empirical-risk objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical-risk definition and qualification concerning unattained minima are sound, but the record has no inspectable source.

children.title: Deterministic Finite-Sum Objectives
children.top_down_role: Covers finite component aggregations independent of a statistical interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Finite-Sum Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite aggregation of fixed component functions, independent of any statistical interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and let \(f_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be fixed component functions for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). A deterministic finite-sum objective is \[F(x):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x),\qquad x\in X,\] on the domain where the extended-real sum is unambiguous. The index set and component functions are deterministic data. An algorithm may sample indices to estimate subgradients or model values, but such sampling does not change the deterministic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic finite-sum objective averages finitely many fixed component functions; randomized index access is an algorithmic device, not part of the objective.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is fixed, and the sum is unambiguous on its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) is a deterministic finite-sum objective.

notation.meaning: Fixed component function indexed by i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic finite-sum definition fits the leaf and correctly separates the objective from randomized algorithmic access, but it lacks a cited source.

children.title: Weighted Component Aggregations
children.top_down_role: Covers nonuniform component weights and their structural role.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Component Aggregations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-weighted finite sums represented as expectations under discrete index sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(f_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and let \(p_i\geq0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\). Define the weighted component aggregation by summing only over the active indices: \[F_p(x):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i f_i(x),\] wherever this extended-real sum is unambiguous. If \(I\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(I=i)=p_i\), then \[F_p(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)].\] Zero-weight components are thereby excluded from the aggregate, and uniform weights recover the arithmetic mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability-weighted component sum over positive-weight indices equals the expectation of the component selected according to those probabilities; uniform probabilities recover the arithmetic mean.
assumptions_latex: The extended-real sum over indices satisfying \(p_i>0\) is unambiguous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_p(x)=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i f_i(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)]\) when \(\mathbb P(I=i)=p_i\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: discrete-expectation identity with zero-weight indices excluded

children.title: Index-Sampling Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Covers how finite components induce stochastic oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Index-Sampling Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between scalar finite-sum objectives and expectations over a discrete component index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(f_1,\ldots,f_n:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and define \(F(x):=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) wherever the sum is unambiguous. If \(I\) is uniform on \(\{1,ldots,n\}\), then \[\mathbb E[f_I(x)]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)=F(x).\] More generally, if \(\mathbb P(I=i)=q_i\) with \(q_i>0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^nq_i=1\), then \[F(x)=\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{f_I(x)}{nq_I}\right],\] whenever the displayed extended-real quantities are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform index sampling represents an arithmetic-mean finite sum exactly; sampling every index with a positive nonuniform probability gives the same objective after inverse-probability weighting.
assumptions_latex: The relevant finite sums and expectations are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)]\) under uniform sampling and \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f_I(x)/(nq_I)]\) under the stated nonuniform sampling.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite discrete expectation and importance-weighting identities

knowledge_statements.title: Streaming Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation objectives accessed sequentially without retaining a predetermined finite dataset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\xi_t)_{t\geq1}\) be a data stream adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\), and let \(f:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). A stationary streaming objective is \[F(x):=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[f(x,\xi)],\] accessed at time \(t\) through the newly arriving observation \(\xi_t\), typically under \(\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P\). Unlike a fixed finite-sum problem, the stream need not have a known terminal sample size or permit repeated component access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A streaming problem accesses an expectation objective through sequentially arriving observations rather than a fixed, repeatedly accessible dataset.
assumptions_latex: For the stationary model, \(\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P\).
\(f(x,\xi)\) is measurable with a well-defined expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E_{P}[f(x,\xi)]\) is accessed through successive observations \(\xi_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes a coherent stationary streaming-access model and fits the topic, but streaming conventions vary and no source establishes this particular conditional-law formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for stochastic integrands on a decision space and measurable sample space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\psi:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) is Carathéodory if \(\psi(\cdot,\xi)\) is continuous on \(X\) for every \(\xi\in\Xi\), and \(\psi(x,\cdot)\) is measurable on \(\Xi\) for every \(x\in X\). It is dominated by an integrable function if there exists a nonnegative measurable function \(g\) such that \(\mathbb E[g(\widetilde\xi)]<\infty\) and \(|\psi(x,\xi)|\leq g(\xi)\) for every \(x\in X\) and almost every \(\xi\in\Xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Carathéodory function is continuous in the decision variable for every sample and measurable in the sample variable for every decision. Integrable domination requires one nonnegative integrable measurable function to bound its absolute value uniformly over decisions, almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi\) is Carathéodory exactly under the stated sectionwise continuity and measurability conditions; integrable domination is defined by the existence of the stated function \(g\).

children.title: Integrand Measurability
children.top_down_role: Covers measurability requirements relevant to stochastic objective representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrand Measurability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise measurability required to form fixed-decision expectations, distinguished from joint measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \((X,\mathcal S)\) be a measurable space, and let \(f:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Pointwise integrand measurability means \[f(x,\cdot):(\Xi,\mathcal A)\longrightarrow(\overline{\mathbb R},\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))\quad\text{is measurable for every }x\in X.\] Under this condition, \(f(x,\xi)\) is an extended-real random variable for each fixed \(x\). Joint measurability with respect to \(\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal A\) is stronger and is a standard sufficient condition for measurability after substituting jointly measurable random decisions and data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each fixed decision, the integrand must be measurable in the random argument; joint measurability is stronger and is a standard sufficient condition for measurable random substitution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed \(x\in X\), \(f(x,\xi)\) is an extended-real random variable.

notation.meaning: Borel sigma-algebra on the extended real line.
Product sigma-algebra on the decision and data spaces.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: measurable-section condition and joint-measurability sufficiency

children.title: Integrability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers integrability conditions supporting finite stochastic objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute, one-sided, and extended-expectation regimes for measurable stochastic integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a measurable extended-real random variable \(Y=f(x,\xi)\), write \(Y^+=\max\{Y,0\}\) and \(Y^-=\max\{-Y,0\}\). It is integrable exactly when \(\mathbb E[Y^+]+\mathbb E[Y^-]<\infty\), equivalently \(\mathbb E|Y|<\infty\), and then \(\mathbb E[Y]\in\mathbb R\). An extended expectation is well-defined when at least one of \(\mathbb E[Y^+]\) and \(\mathbb E[Y^-]\) is finite, in which case \[\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[Y^+]-\mathbb E[Y^-]\in\overline{\mathbb R}.\] If both parts have infinite expectation, the expectation is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute integrability gives a finite expectation; one-sided integrability permits an extended value; two infinite parts make the expectation undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(Y=f(x,\xi)\) is an extended-real measurable random variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Y]\) is finite under \(L^1\)-integrability and extended-real under one-sided integrability, but undefined for \(\mathbb E[Y^+]=\mathbb E[Y^-]=\infty\).

notation.meaning: Class of absolutely integrable random variables.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite, one-sided extended, and undefined expectation regimes are correctly distinguished, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Expectation Interchange Principles
children.top_down_role: Covers justified interchange operations used in stochastic analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Interchange Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominated-convergence criterion for interchanging an almost-sure pointwise limit and expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, and let \(Y,Y_1,Y_2,\ldots:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be measurable random variables such that \(Y_k\to Y\) almost surely. If there exists an integrable random variable \(G:\Omega\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(|Y_k|\leq G\) almost surely for every \(k\), then \(Y\) is integrable and \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb E[Y_k]=\mathbb E\!\left[\lim_{k\to\infty}Y_k\right]=\mathbb E[Y].\] In particular, taking \(Y_k=f(x_k,\xi)\) permits passage of a decision-sequence limit through expectation when the stated measurability, convergence, and domination hypotheses hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For measurable random variables, almost-sure convergence together with a common integrable dominator makes the limit integrable and permits interchange of limit and expectation.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(Y,Y_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) are measurable.
There exists an integrable \(G:\Omega\to[0,\infty)\) with \(|Y_k|\leq G\) almost surely for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y\) is integrable and \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbb E[Y_k]=\mathbb E[Y]\).

notation.meaning: Sequence of measurable real-valued random variables.
Common nonnegative integrable dominating random variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of semismoothness and strong semismoothness under integrable sample-dependent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N\) be a neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Suppose \(\psi(\cdot,\xi)\) is B-differentiable on \(\mathcal N\) for almost every \(\xi\), and suppose there is a positive random variable \(L(\xi)\) with \(\mathbb E[L(\widetilde\xi)]<\infty\) such that \(|\psi(x,\xi)-\psi(x',\xi)|\leq L(\xi)\|x-x'\|\) for all \(x,x'\) near \(\bar x\), almost surely. For \(\varphi(x)=\mathbb E[\psi(x,\widetilde\xi)]\): (a) if \(\psi(\cdot,\xi)\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) almost surely, then \(\varphi\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\); (b) if there exists a positive random variable \(L'(\xi)\) with \(\mathbb E[L'(\widetilde\xi)]<\infty\) such that, almost surely, \[\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{|\psi'(x;x-\bar x,\xi)-\psi'(\bar x;x-\bar x,\xi)|}{\|x-\bar x\|^2}\leq L'(\xi),\] then \(\varphi\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an integrable local Lipschitz modulus, samplewise semismoothness passes to the expectation. Strong semismoothness also passes when the quadratic directional-derivative remainder has an integrable sample-dependent bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\psi(\cdot,\xi)\text{ is B-differentiable on a neighborhood of }\bar x\text{ for a.e. }\xi\)
\(\mathbb E[L(\widetilde\xi)]<\infty\) and \(|\psi(x,\xi)-\psi(x',\xi)|\leq L(\xi)\|x-x'\|\) locally, almost surely
For part (b), \(\mathbb E[L'(\widetilde\xi)]<\infty\) and the stated quadratic limsup bound holds almost surely
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi(\cdot,\xi)\text{ semismooth a.s.}\Rightarrow\varphi\text{ semismooth at }\bar x\); the additional integrably bounded strong-semismoothness condition implies that \(\varphi\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\).

children.title: Exceptional-Set Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Covers null-set and version issues that affect oracle interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Exceptional-Set Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise almost-sure assertions need not share one exceptional null set over uncountable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\Xi=[0,1]\), let \(\xi\) be uniformly distributed, and define \(f(x,\xi):=\mathbf 1_{\{\xi=x\}}\). For every fixed \(x\in X\), \(f(x,\xi)=0\) almost surely and \(\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]=0\). Nevertheless, for every realization \(z\in[0,1]\), choosing \(x=z\) gives \(f(z,z)=1\). Hence there is no single probability-one event on which \(f(x,\xi)=0\) holds simultaneously for all \(x\in X\). Pointwise almost-sure statements therefore cannot be made uniform over uncountable decision sets without additional regularity or separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Null sets may depend on the decision: pointwise almost-sure validity does not imply simultaneous validity over an uncountable decision set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f(x,\xi)=0\) almost surely for each fixed \(x\), no common probability-one event makes this equality hold for every \(x\).

notation.meaning: Indicator of the event or set A.
Uniform random element of the unit interval.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal indicator is a valid counterexample and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the stated boundary principle.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstructured Weakly Convex Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real formulation without assumed composite structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(f\) is called unstructured \(\rho\)-weakly convex when \[x\longmapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\] is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(y)+\frac{\rho}{2}t(1-t)\lVert x-y\rVert^2.\] Here unstructured means that no additive, compositional, or max-value representation is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unstructured objective is rho-weakly convex when adding a quadratic of curvature rho makes it convex, without assuming an additive, compositional, or max-value representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Composite Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive weakly convex loss plus an extended-real convex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[F(x)=g(x)+r(x).\] Then \(F\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex. In particular, choosing \(r=\delta_C\) for a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) represents a convex constraint without changing the weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a proper lower-semicontinuous convex regularizer, including a closed convex constraint indicator, to a rho-weakly convex loss preserves the same weak-convexity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=g+r\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Composite Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean finite-dimensional convex-outer, smooth-inner composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) by \[F(x)=h(G(x)).\] Then \(F\) is \(L_hL_G\)-weakly convex; equivalently, \[x\longmapsto h(G(x))+\frac{L_hL_G}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\] is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex Lipschitz outer function composed with a continuously differentiable mapping having a Lipschitz Jacobian is weakly convex with modulus equal to the product of the two Lipschitz constants.
assumptions_latex: \(G:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable, and its Jacobian is \(L_G\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean operator norm.
\(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(L_h\)-Lipschitz on a convex set containing \(G(\mathbb{R}^d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ G\) is \(L_hL_G\)-weakly convex.

children.title: Finite Max-Type Objectives
children.top_down_role: Covers objectives formed from finite collections of competing components.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Max-Type Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise maxima of weakly convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar\rho=\max_{1\le i\le m}\rho_i\) and define \[F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x),\qquad I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=F(x)\}.\] Then \(F\) is \(\bar\rho\)-weakly convex, and \(I(x)\) is its active index set at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of weakly convex functions is weakly convex with modulus equal to the largest component modulus, and its active indices are those attaining the maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) is \(\bar\rho\)-weakly convex for \(\bar\rho=\max_{1\le i\le m}\rho_i\).

notation.meaning: active index set at a point

children.title: Parameterized Value Functions
children.top_down_role: Covers objectives induced by optimizing over latent parameters.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(Y\) is a nonempty parameter set.
\(\Phi:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has a nonempty argmax whenever the value is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\) with solution mapping \(S(x)=\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper value functions appropriate to max-value weakly convex models.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Value Functions Associated with Convex Functions p. 268
5.7 Some Nonconvex Stochastic Value Functions p. 292

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The parameterized upper value function generated by \(\Phi\) and \(Y\) is \[V(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y),\qquad x\in X.\] Its solution mapping is \[S(x)=\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)=\{y\in Y:\Phi(x,y)=V(x)\}.\] When the supremum is attained, \(V(x)=\max_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\). Finite max-type objectives are recovered by taking \(Y=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(\Phi(x,i)=f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized upper value function takes the supremum of a payoff over parameters, while its solution mapping records the maximizing parameters.

children.title: Active-Index Stability
children.top_down_role: Covers stability regimes for active components or latent optimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer semicontinuity of the active set for finite continuous maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x),\qquad I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=F(x)\}.\] There exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Thus no index inactive at \(\bar x\) can become active arbitrarily close to \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite maximum of functions continuous near the reference point, every sufficiently nearby active index was already active at the reference point.
assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous near \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\) for every \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\).
\(|F(x)-F(y)|\le L\lVert x-y\rVert\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Euclidean Lipschitz regularity for finite-valued objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(F\) lies in the globally \(L\)-Lipschitz regime when \[|F(x)-F(y)|\le L\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\] If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz, this condition is equivalent to the uniform generalized-gradient bound \[\lVert v\rVert\le L\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^d\text{ and }v\in\partial_C F(x),\] where \(\partial_C F\) denotes the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The globally Lipschitz regime uses one finite constant to bound every objective difference, equivalently all Clarke subgradients when the objective is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.title: Globally Lipschitz Regime

children.title: Local Lipschitz Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers regularity confined to neighborhoods relevant to the iterates.

assumptions_latex: The reference point \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is Lipschitz on some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise local Euclidean Lipschitz regularity with neighborhood-dependent constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(F\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x\) if there exist constants \(r_{\bar x}>0\) and \(L_{\bar x}<\infty\) such that \[|F(x)-F(y)|\le L_{\bar x}\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in B(\bar x,r_{\bar x}).\] It is locally Lipschitz on a set \(D\) when this condition holds at every \(\bar x\in D\), with constants and radii allowed to depend on \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz regularity bounds objective differences only inside a neighborhood of each reference point, with constants that may vary across the domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Regimes

children.title: Growth-Controlled Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers objective or oracle behavior controlled through state-dependent growth.

assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\xi)\) is a measurable stochastic generalized-gradient oracle.
A nondecreasing function \(q:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) and constants \(a,b\ge0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert G(x,\xi)\rVert^2\mid x]\le a+bq(\lVert x\rVert)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-moment oracle growth replacing a uniform global Lipschitz bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic oracle lies in a \(q\)-growth-controlled regime when, for every query point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert G(x,\xi)\rVert^2\mid x\right]\le a+bq(\lVert x\rVert).\] The common quadratic-growth specialization is \(q(t)=t^2\). Unlike a globally bounded second moment, this condition permits oracle magnitudes to increase with the iterate norm; convergence arguments must therefore also control the moments of the iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A growth-controlled oracle may become larger away from the origin, but its conditional second moment is bounded by a prescribed function of the iterate norm.

children.title: Iterate Localization
children.top_down_role: Covers mechanisms that keep local regularity applicable.

assumptions_latex: An iterative method produces random iterates \((x_k)_{k\ge0}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(x_k\in K\text{ for all }k)=1\), or a stated high-probability analogue.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stopping-time localization is the standard device for applying local regularity along stochastic iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment condition needed to use local regularity constants along an entire stochastic trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed region \(K\), define the exit time \[\tau_K=\inf\{k\ge0:x_k\notin K\},\qquad\inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Almost-sure iterate localization means \(\mathbb{P}(\tau_K=+\infty)=1\). A finite-horizon high-probability version specifies \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and requires \[\mathbb{P}(\tau_K>N)\ge1-\delta.\] On the corresponding event, every local Lipschitz, weak-convexity, or oracle-moment bound valid uniformly on \(K\) applies to all queried iterates through time \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Localization requires all iterates, or all iterates up to a horizon with high probability, to remain inside the region where local regularity bounds hold.

children.title: Escape-from-Region Failures

knowledge_statements.title: Escape-from-Region Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete escape showing that local Lipschitz regularity alone does not localize iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(x)=-x^2\). This function is \(2\)-weakly convex and locally Lipschitz but is not globally Lipschitz. For constant-step gradient descent with \(\alpha>0\) and \(x_0\ne0\), the iterates satisfy \[x_k=(1+2\alpha)^k x_0\] and therefore \[|x_k|\longrightarrow+\infty.\] Consequently, every bounded interval containing \(x_0\) is eventually exited, so local regularity alone does not ensure iterate localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the locally Lipschitz, weakly convex function minus x squared, constant-step gradient descent diverges from every nonzero starting point and eventually leaves every bounded localization region.
assumptions_latex: Gradient descent uses a constant step \(\alpha>0\) and starts from \(x_0\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|x_k|=(1+2\alpha)^k|x_0|\to+\infty\), so every bounded interval containing \(x_0\) is eventually exited.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Proximal Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean proximal map and Moreau envelope for a weakly convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex. For \(\lambda>0\), define
\[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x):=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},\qquad f_\lambda(x):=\min_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.\]
If \(0<\lambda<\rho^{-1}\), with \(\rho^{-1}=+\infty\) when \(\rho=0\), the minimized function is strongly convex; hence the proximal point is unique and \(\nabla f_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic regularization defines the Euclidean proximal point and Moreau envelope; below the weak-convexity threshold, the proximal point is unique and yields the envelope gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) is single-valued and \(\nabla f_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\).

children.title: Bregman Proximal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Covers proximal constructions induced by non-Euclidean reference kernels.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Proximal Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bregman proximal map generated by a differentiable convex kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex, let \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and let \(h:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, strictly convex, and differentiable on \(U\). For \(x\in U\) and \(y\in\operatorname{dom}h\), set
\[D_h(y,x):=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle.\]
Given a proper function \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\lambda>0\), its Bregman proximal mapping at \(x\) is
\[\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda f}(x):=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{y\in C}\left\{f(y)+\lambda^{-1}D_h(y,x)\right\}.\]
The mapping is defined wherever this minimizer set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman proximal point minimizes the objective plus a divergence generated by a differentiable strictly convex kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, strictly convex, and differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda f}(x)=\operatorname{argmin}_{y\in C}\{f(y)+\lambda^{-1}D_h(y,x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the kernel

children.title: Relative Weak Convexity
children.top_down_role: Covers weak convexity measured relative to a reference kernel.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Weak Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convexity measured relative to a convex kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex, and let \(f,h:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper functions with \(h\) convex. The function \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex relative to \(h\), for \(\rho\geq0\), when \(f+\rho h\) is convex on \(C\). If \(h\) is differentiable at \(x\in C\), this implies the local support inequality
\[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-\rho D_h(y,x)\]
for every admissible relative subgradient \(v\) at \(x\) and every \(y\in C\). For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\lVert x\rVert^2\), this reduces to ordinary Euclidean \(\rho\)-weak convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative weak convexity means that adding a nonnegative multiple of the kernel makes the objective convex; the quadratic kernel recovers ordinary weak convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) are proper, and \(h\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex relative to \(h\) exactly when \(f+\rho h\) is convex on \(C\).

children.title: Kernel Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers alignment between the objective, domain, and reference geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions making a Bregman proximal subproblem finite and solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex set \(C\), proper objective \(f\), kernel \(h\), center \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and \(\lambda>0\), call \((f,h,C)\) kernel-compatible at \((x,\lambda)\) when
\[C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}h\neq\varnothing\]
and the function
\[y\mapsto f(y)+\lambda^{-1}D_h(y,x)+\delta_C(y)\]
is proper, lower semicontinuous, and level-bounded. A sufficient curvature regime is that \(f+\rho h\) is convex and \(0<\lambda<\rho^{-1}\), together with level-boundedness. Under compatibility, the Bregman proximal value is finite and its minimizer set is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernel compatibility requires overlapping domains and a proper, lower-semicontinuous, level-bounded proximal objective, ensuring existence and compactness of Bregman proximal points.
assumptions_latex: \(f+\lambda^{-1}D_h(\cdot,x)+\delta_C\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and level-bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}_{y\in C}\{f(y)+\lambda^{-1}D_h(y,x)\}\) is nonempty and compact.

children.title: Boundary-Degenerate Geometry
children.top_down_role: Covers failures caused by singular or poorly conditioned reference geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Degenerate Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of kernel-centered proximal geometry at domain boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\mathbb{R}^d_+\) and let the entropy kernel be
\[h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d x_i\log x_i,\]
with \(0\log0=0\). Although \(h\) is finite on \(C\), its gradient is defined only on \(\mathbb{R}^d_{++}\). If a proximal center \(x\in C\) has \(x_i=0\) for some \(i\), then \(\nabla h(x)\) and consequently \(D_h(y,x)\) in the gradient-based formula are undefined. Thus an algorithm requiring Bregman steps centered at every feasible point cannot be extended to this boundary without a modified divergence, an interior-preserving rule, or limiting conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For entropy geometry, boundary centers have no finite kernel gradient, so the usual Bregman divergence and proximal step are undefined there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h(x)\) and the standard gradient-based quantity \(D_h(y,x)\) are undefined.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entropy-boundary example correctly targets a failure boundary and clearly distinguishes the closed kernel domain from the differentiability domain. No source is supplied for certification of the boundary-degenerate Bregman convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex feasible sets and their Euclidean projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed convex constraint in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(H\) is a feasible set \(C\subseteq H\) that is nonempty, closed, and convex. Its indicator is
\[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\]
and its Euclidean projection is
\[P_C(x)=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{y\in C}\lVert y-x\rVert.\]
For every \(x\in H\), the projection exists and is unique, and it is characterized by
\[p=P_C(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\in C\ \text{and}\ \langle x-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\ \text{for all }y\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex feasible set has a unique Euclidean projection characterized by the standard variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(x)\) exists uniquely for every \(x\in H\) and satisfies the projection variational inequality.

notation.meaning: indicator function of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Proximally Smooth Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform single-valued projection in a neighborhood of a constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty closed set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is \(r\)-proximally smooth, or has reach at least \(r>0\), when every point \(x\) satisfying
\[0<\operatorname{dist}(x,C)<r\]
has a unique nearest point in \(C\). Equivalently, the metric projection
\[P_C(x):=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{y\in C}\lVert x-y\rVert\]
is single-valued throughout the open \(r\)-tube around \(C\). This property permits locally well-defined projected or proximal updates even though \(C\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximally smooth set has a unique nearest-point projection throughout a fixed tubular neighborhood, despite possibly being nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(x)\) is single-valued whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)<r\).

children.title: Manifold Constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local equality representation and tangent-normal geometry of a smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be an embedded \(C^1\) manifold of codimension \(m\). For every \(\bar x\in M\), there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a \(C^1\) mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(F(\bar x)=0\), \(\nabla F(x)\) has rank \(m\) on \(M\cap U\), and
\[M\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)=0\}.\]
At \(\bar x\), its tangent and normal spaces are
\[T_M(\bar x)=\ker\nabla F(\bar x),\qquad N_M(\bar x)=\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth embedded manifold is locally a full-rank equality set; its tangent space is the Jacobian kernel and its normal space the adjoint range.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is an embedded \(C^1\) manifold of codimension \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) admits a local full-rank equation representation, with \(T_M(\bar x)=\ker\nabla F(\bar x)\) and \(N_M(\bar x)=\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex. A weakly convex inequality system consists of functions \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,m\), for which there are constants \(\rho_i\geq0\) such that
\[x\mapsto g_i(x)+\frac{\rho_i}{2}\lVert x\rVert^2\]
is convex on \(X\). Its feasible set is
\[C=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}.\]
Although each defining function is weakly convex, \(C\) need not be convex. Weak convexity of the defining functions alone does not imply convex-set projection properties or unrestricted normal-cone intersection formulas for \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly convex inequality constraints are sublevel conditions of functions made convex by adding quadratic curvature. Their common feasible set may be nonconvex, so convex projection and unrestricted normal-cone calculus do not follow from weak convexity alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Constraint Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transversality condition for intersecting manifold and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[C=M\cap\{x:g_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\},\]
where \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a \(C^1\) manifold and each \(g_i\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\in C\). With active set \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\), a mixed transversality condition at \(\bar x\) is
\[v+\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i z_i=0,\quad v\in N_M(\bar x),\quad z_i\in\partial g_i(\bar x),\quad \lambda_i\geq0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v=0\ \text{and}\ \lambda_i=0\ \text{for all }i.\]
It excludes cancellation between manifold normals and active inequality normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed transversality forbids a nontrivial cancellation between a manifold normal and nonnegative combinations of active inequality subgradients.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a \(C^1\) manifold and \(\bar x\in C\).
Each \(g_i\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v+\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i z_i=0\) implies \(v=0\) and \(\lambda_i=0\) for every active index.

children.title: Constraint-Qualification Failures
children.top_down_role: Covers degeneracies that obstruct stable constraint certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Qualification Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of normal-cone intersection calculus without transversality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), let
\[C_1=\{(u,v):v\geq u^2\},\qquad C_2=\{(u,v):v\leq-u^2\}.\]
Both sets are closed and convex, and \(C_1\cap C_2=\{(0,0)\}\). At the origin,
\[N_{C_1}(0,0)=\{(0,-a):a\geq0\},\qquad N_{C_2}(0,0)=\{(0,a):a\geq0\},\]
so nonzero opposite normals exist and the transversality condition fails. Moreover,
\[N_{C_1}(0,0)+N_{C_2}(0,0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\neq\mathbb{R}^2=N_{C_1\cap C_2}(0,0).\]
Thus the usual normal-cone intersection formula fails without a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two tangent convex regions intersect only at the origin; opposite normals violate transversality, and the normal cone of the intersection exceeds the sum of normals.
assumptions_latex: Normal cones are convex-analytic normal cones.
