knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-Gradient Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-envelope gradient norm as a smooth stationarity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex. For \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), define \(f_\lambda(x)=\min_y\{f(y)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\}\) and \(y_\lambda(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). Then \(f_\lambda\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla f_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-y_\lambda(x))\). Thus \(\lVert\nabla f_\lambda(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\) is a computable envelope-stationarity certificate, and equality to zero is equivalent to \(0\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weakly convex function, the Moreau-envelope gradient equals scaled proximal displacement and vanishes exactly at stationary points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\), and \(\nabla f_\lambda(x)=0\iff0\in\partial f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Displacement Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance to the proximal point as an equivalent envelope certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the weak-convexity assumptions for the Moreau envelope, let \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). The proximal displacement \(d_\lambda(x)=\lVert x-y\rVert\) satisfies \(d_\lambda(x)=\lambda\lVert\nabla f_\lambda(x)\rVert\). Hence \(d_\lambda(x)\leq\lambda\varepsilon\) certifies \(\lVert\nabla f_\lambda(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\). Moreover, proximal optimality gives \(\lambda^{-1}(x-y)\in\partial f(y)\), so the same displacement supplies a subgradient of norm \(d_\lambda(x)/\lambda\) at the nearby point \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small proximal displacement is exactly equivalent to a small envelope gradient and produces a small subgradient at the proximal point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_\lambda(x)=\lambda\lVert\nabla f_\lambda(x)\rVert\) and \(\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\in\partial f(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nearby-Point Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Envelope stationarity transferred to a nearby proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, choose \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), and set \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). If \(\lVert\nabla f_\lambda(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon\), then \(\lVert x-y\rVert\leq\lambda\varepsilon\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(y))\leq\varepsilon\). Thus an envelope-stationary point \(x\) certifies the existence of an ordinary approximately stationary point \(y\) within distance \(\lambda\varepsilon\); specifically, \(\lambda^{-1}(x-y)\in\partial f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small envelope gradient at x yields a nearby proximal point y having an ordinary subgradient of the same small norm.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x-y\rVert\leq\lambda\varepsilon\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(y))\leq\varepsilon\) for \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\).

notation.meaning: Nearby proximal point associated with x.
Distance from zero to the subdifferential at y.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial(f+r)(T_\alpha(x)))\le (1+\alpha L)\|G_\alpha(x)\|.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean composite model with a smooth term and a convex proximable term.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 The proximal gradient method for convex programs p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_\alpha(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha r}(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))\) and \(G_\alpha(x)=\alpha^{-1}(x-T_\alpha(x))\). Proximal optimality gives
\[G_\alpha(x)-\nabla f(x)\in\partial r(T_\alpha(x)).\]
Consequently,
\[G_\alpha(x)+\nabla f(T_\alpha(x))-\nabla f(x)\in\partial(f+r)(T_\alpha(x)),\]
and Lipschitz continuity yields
\[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial(f+r)(T_\alpha(x)))\le(1+\alpha L)\|G_\alpha(x)\|.\]
Thus a small mapping norm certifies approximate stationarity at the updated point; \(G_\alpha(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(0\in\partial(f+r)(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal-gradient mapping bounds a genuine composite subgradient at the updated point, and its vanishing is exactly equivalent to composite stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Gradient Mapping Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5.2 The proximal gradient method for convex programs p. 93

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate is mathematically standard, but the cited locator is explicitly for convex programs while the record allows nonconvex smooth f. Full-text support for that broader scope is needed. The statement also contains a derivation and does not specify the subdifferential used.

assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(r:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper closed convex functions.
The displayed convex model has a minimizer for \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial m_x(x^+))\le\|G_t(x)\|.\]
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the prox-linear model residual and its qualification-dependent subdifferential formula.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for the convexly regularized linearized model, not automatically for the original composite at the same point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[m_x(y)=h(c(x)+Dc(x)(y-x))+r(y),\qquad x^+\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\left\{m_x(y)+\frac{1}{2t}\|y-x\|^2\right\},\]
and \(G_t(x)=t^{-1}(x-x^+)\). Convex optimality implies
\[G_t(x)\in\partial m_x(x^+),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial m_x(x^+))\le\|G_t(x)\|.\]
Hence \(\|G_t(x)\|\) is a verifiable stationarity certificate for the prox-linear model. Moreover, \(G_t(x)=0\) implies \(0\in\partial m_x(x)\); under the standard convex-composite chain and sum qualification, this is equivalent to \(0\in Dc(x)^*\partial h(c(x))+\partial r(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled prox-linear step is a model subgradient, so its norm certifies model stationarity; at a zero step, qualified composite stationarity follows.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Linear Residual Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The model-residual certificate fits the leaf, but no citation supports the prox-linear construction or the qualification-dependent chain-and-sum formula. The statement also includes proof-style derivation.

children.title: Projected Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covers stationarity measures based on projection operators.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_\alpha^C(x)-\nabla f(x)\in N_C(z).\]
review_flags: No supplied locator precisely states the projected-gradient residual certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[z=P_C(x-\alpha\nabla f(x)),\qquad G_\alpha^C(x)=\frac{x-z}{\alpha}.\]
The projection characterization gives
\[x-\alpha\nabla f(x)-z\in N_C(z),\]
which is equivalently
\[G_\alpha^C(x)-\nabla f(x)\in N_C(z).\]
Thus the projected residual directly supplies a normal vector at the projected point. In particular, \(G_\alpha^C(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in\nabla f(x)+N_C(x)\), so a zero projected residual exactly certifies first-order constrained stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected-gradient step produces an explicit normal vector at the projected point, and a zero projected residual is exactly constrained stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Residual Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-residual formula and zero-residual equivalence are correct for a closed convex set and fit the certificate container, but no inspectable source is supplied and the statement includes derivation.

children.title: Normal-Cone Residual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covers stationarity measures expressed through normal-cone geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r_N(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\nabla f(x)+N_C(x).\]
review_flags: No supplied locator precisely supports this normal-cone residual formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-form certificate for smooth optimization over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the normal-cone residual by
\[r_N(x)=\operatorname{dist}(-
abla f(x),N_C(x))=\inf_{v\in N_C(x)}\|
abla f(x)+v\|.\]
Every \(v\in N_C(x)\) produces the verifiable stationarity candidate \(
abla f(x)+v\). Therefore \(r_N(x)\le\varepsilon\) means that such candidates can be found with norm arbitrarily close to \(\varepsilon\); if the distance is attained, one has a vector of norm at most \(\varepsilon\). Since the convex normal cone is closed,
\[r_N(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in
abla f(x)+N_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance from the negative gradient to the normal cone measures constrained first-order stationarity and vanishes exactly at stationary points.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Residual Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance residual is mathematically appropriate for this certificate leaf, but it lacks a cited source and includes explanatory proof text.

children.title: Residual Correspondence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers conditions under which the two certificate forms align.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood containing \(x\) and \(z=P_C(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|G_\alpha^C(x)\|\le r_N(x),\qquad r_N(z)\le(1+\alpha L)\|G_\alpha^C(x)\|.\]
review_flags: No supplied source locator states both comparison inequalities in this regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided correspondence uses convex projection geometry and compares residuals at different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z=P_C(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))\). Nonexpansiveness of \(P_C\), together with \(x=P_C(x+\alpha v)\) for every \(v\in N_C(x)\), yields
\[\|G_\alpha^C(x)\|\le r_N(x).\]
Projection optimality also gives \(G_\alpha^C(x)-\nabla f(x)\in N_C(z)\). Hence
\[r_N(z)\le\|G_\alpha^C(x)+\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(x)\|\le(1+\alpha L)\|G_\alpha^C(x)\|.\]
Thus projected and normal-cone residuals correspond quantitatively for closed convex constraints, with the forward comparison naturally evaluated at the projected point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex constraints, the projected residual is bounded by the normal residual at the current point and controls the normal residual at the projected point.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Correspondence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both comparison inequalities are correct in the stated convex regime and the property kind fits the correspondence leaf, but no source supports them and the statement presents their derivation.

children.title: Nonconvex-Constraint Limitations
children.top_down_role: Covers certificate limitations beyond stable convex projection regimes.

assumptions_latex: The normal cone is the Mordukhovich limiting normal cone.
Euclidean projection onto a nonconvex closed set may be set-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r_N(1)=0\quad\text{but}\quad\|G_\alpha^C(1)\|=2/\alpha>0\quad(\alpha>1).\]
review_flags: A source for the precise limiting-normal versus projection counterexample is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of projected and limiting-normal residual equivalence for a disconnected constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb{R}\), \(f(u)=u\), and \(x=1\). Because \(x\) is isolated in \(C\), the limiting normal cone is \(N_C(1)=\mathbb{R}\). Consequently,
\[r_N(1)=\operatorname{dist}(-1,N_C(1))=0.\]
For every \(\alpha>1\), the point \(1-\alpha\) is strictly closer to \(-1\) than to \(1\), so \(P_C(1-\alpha)= -1\) and
\[\|G_\alpha^C(1)\|=\frac{|1-(-1)|}{\alpha}=\frac{2}{\alpha}>0.\]
Thus limiting-normal stationarity need not imply a zero projected residual once convexity of the constraint is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a disconnected set, limiting-normal stationarity can be vacuous while a projected step remains nonzero, so convex residual correspondence fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex-Constraint Limitations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disconnected-set counterexample is internally correct and the counterexample kind precisely fits the limitation leaf, but it has no cited source and is written as a calculation-based proof.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold and \(R_x\) is a retraction defined near \(0\in T_xM\).
\(F:M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and its pullback is subdifferentiable at the selected step.
The displayed regularized pullback problem has a minimizer \(\eta_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial(F\circ R_x)(\eta_t))\le\|G_t^R(x)\|.\]
review_flags: The supplied inventory has no manifold-retraction source supporting this pullback certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space proximal certificate for a nonsmooth objective pulled back through a retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), choose
\[\eta_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in T_xM}\left\{(F\circ R_x)(\eta)+\frac{1}{2t}\|\eta\|_x^2\right\},\qquad G_t^R(x)=-\frac{\eta_t}{t}.\]
The first-order condition for the regularized pullback problem is
\[G_t^R(x)\in\partial(F\circ R_x)(\eta_t).\]
Therefore
\[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial(F\circ R_x)(\eta_t))\le\|G_t^R(x)\|.\]
The residual is consequently a stationarity certificate for the pullback at the tangent step. If \(G_t^R(x)=0\), then \(\eta_t=0\) and \(0\in\partial(F\circ R_x)(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled regularized tangent step is a pullback subgradient, so its norm certifies stationarity of the retracted local model.
knowledge_statements.title: Retraction-Based Residual Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pullback certificate requires a source specifying the manifold pullback subdifferential and the applicable Fermat/sum rule. The current subdifferential is unspecified, and the statement contains a derivation.

children.title: Envelope Stationarity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covers stationarity measured through envelope geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Stationarity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-envelope certificate below the weak-convexity smoothing threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[\varphi_\lambda(x)=\inf_y\left\{\varphi(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\},\qquad x_\lambda=\operatorname*{argmin}_y\left\{\varphi(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}.\]
The proximal point is unique, \(\varphi_\lambda\) is continuously differentiable, and
\[\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)=\frac{x-x_\lambda}{\lambda}.\]
Thus \(\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|\) is an envelope stationarity certificate, with
\[\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|=\lambda^{-1}\|x-x_\lambda\|,\qquad \nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ 0\in\partial\varphi(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below the weak-convexity threshold, the Moreau-envelope gradient equals the scaled proximal displacement and vanishes exactly at limiting-subgradient stationary points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|=\lambda^{-1}\|x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\varphi}(x)\|.\]

children.title: Subgradient Stationarity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covers stationarity measured through subgradient residuals.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r_\partial(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\partial\varphi(x).\]
review_flags: No supplied locator precisely defines the limiting-subgradient stationarity certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise stationarity certificate based on the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[r_\partial(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x))=\inf_{v\in\partial\varphi(x)}\|v\|,\]
with \(r_\partial(x)=+\infty\) when \(\partial\varphi(x)=\varnothing\). The point \(x\) is called \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient-stationary when \(r_\partial(x)\le\varepsilon\). Because the limiting subdifferential is closed whenever it is nonempty,
\[r_\partial(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\partial\varphi(x).\]
Thus the residual measures stationarity at the reported point itself, unlike certificates whose subgradient conclusion holds only at a nearby proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradient stationarity is the distance from zero to the limiting subdifferential at the reported point and is exact when that distance vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Stationarity Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limiting-subgradient distance is the correct certificate for this leaf, but no citation is supplied and the closedness argument constitutes proof text.

children.title: Nearby-Point Certificate Transfer
children.top_down_role: Covers transfer between envelope points and nearby subgradient certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearby-Point Certificate Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact transfer from an envelope gradient at \(x\) to a limiting subgradient at its proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_\lambda=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\varphi}(x)\) and \(g_\lambda=\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\). Then
\[g_\lambda=\frac{x-x_\lambda}{\lambda}\in\partial\varphi(x_\lambda),\]
and consequently
\[\|x-x_\lambda\|=\lambda\|g_\lambda\|,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x_\lambda))\le\|g_\lambda\|.\]
In particular, \(\|g_\lambda\|\le\varepsilon\) certifies an \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient-stationary point within distance \(\lambda\varepsilon\) of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small envelope gradient produces an equally small limiting subgradient at the proximal point, which is at most the smoothing parameter times the certificate size away.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|x-x_\lambda\|=\lambda\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x_\lambda))\le\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|.\]

children.title: Certificate Nonequivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Covers regimes where the certificate notions cannot be interchanged.

assumptions_latex: A fixed smoothing parameter \(\lambda>0\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x_k)\|\to0\quad\text{while}\quad\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x_k))=1.\]
review_flags: The exact counterexample is standard but is not specifically supported by a supplied locator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Envelope stationarity at a point does not imply subgradient stationarity at that same point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\lambda>0\), let \(\varphi(u)=|u|\), and set \(x_k=\lambda/(k+1)>0\). Since \(0<x_k<\lambda\), soft thresholding gives \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\varphi}(x_k)=0\), and hence
\[\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x_k)\|=\frac{x_k}{\lambda}=\frac{1}{k+1}\longrightarrow0.\]
However, \(\partial\varphi(x_k)=\{1\}\) for every \(k\), so
\[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x_k))=1.\]
Therefore a small envelope-gradient certificate at \(x_k\) need not imply a small subgradient residual at that same point; the valid transfer is to the nearby proximal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the absolute value, envelope gradients can approach zero at positive points whose same-point subgradient residual remains one.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Nonequivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute-value example correctly establishes same-point nonequivalence and the counterexample kind fits the boundary leaf, but no source is cited and the statement includes the calculation proving the example.

children.title: Stationarity Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Covers accuracy expressed through stationarity certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Envelope-based stationarity accuracy for weakly convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x\) has envelope stationarity accuracy \(\varepsilon\) at scale \(\lambda\) when
\[\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|\le\varepsilon.\]
For \(x_\lambda=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\varphi}(x)\), this condition guarantees
\[\|x-x_\lambda\|\le\lambda\varepsilon,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x_\lambda))\le\varepsilon.\]
This condition concerns first-order stationarity and does not, without an additional growth or error-bound assumption, imply objective-value accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Envelope stationarity accuracy bounds both the limiting-subgradient residual at the associated proximal point and the distance to that point, but it does not alone imply objective-value accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|\nabla\varphi_\lambda(x)\|\le\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \|x-x_\lambda\|\le\lambda\varepsilon\ \text{ and }\ \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\varphi(x_\lambda))\le\varepsilon.\]

children.title: Objective-Value Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Covers accuracy expressed through objective gaps or excess risk.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines global objective accuracy relative to the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and bounded below, and set \(F^\star:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}F(x)\). For \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), a point \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) is \(\varepsilon\)-accurate in objective value when
\[
F(x)-F^\star\le \varepsilon.
\]
For a random output \(X\), expected objective-value accuracy means \(\mathbb{E}[F(X)-F^\star]\le\varepsilon\), while \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-high-confidence accuracy means \(\mathbb{P}(F(X)-F^\star\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-value accuracy bounds the output’s global suboptimality, either deterministically, in expectation, or with a stated failure probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)-F^\star\le\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Objective-Value Accuracy leaf and is mathematically standard, but no source reference or inspectable locator is supplied. The random-output variants also require measurability of F(X), which should be made explicit when sourced.

children.title: Geometry-Based Accuracy Transfer
children.top_down_role: Covers geometric regimes that connect the two accuracy notions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(x)\le\eta\Longrightarrow F(x)-F^\star\le C\eta^p\).

notation.meaning: region where the geometric bound holds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers a stationarity residual to objective accuracy under explicit growth geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its minimum on the nonempty set \(X^\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}F(x)\), and set \(F^\star:=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}F(x)\). Let \(s:\operatorname{dom}F\to[0,+\infty]\) be a stationarity residual. Suppose that for a region \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}F\) and constants \(C>0\) and \(p>0\),
\[
F(x)-F^\star\le C s(x)^p\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
Then, for every \(\eta\ge0\), each \(x\in D\) satisfying \(s(x)\le\eta\) obeys
\[
F(x)-F^\star\le C\eta^p.
\]
For a random output \(X\) taking values in \(D\), the event \(\{s(X)\le\eta\}\) is contained in the event \(\{F(X)-F^\star\le C\eta^p\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated geometric error bound, every stationarity tolerance eta transfers to the objective-gap tolerance C times eta to the power p, including eventwise for a random output in the region.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Based Accuracy Transfer

children.title: Accuracy-Transfer Failures
children.top_down_role: Covers nonconvex regimes where small stationarity need not imply objective quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Transfer Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that even exact stationarity need not imply global objective accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(F(x)=(x^2-1)^2\). Since \(F''(x)=12x^2-4\ge-4\), the function is \(4\)-weakly convex. At \(x=0\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(0))=|F'(0)|=0,
\qquad
F(0)-\inf_{z\in\mathbb{R}}F(z)=1.
\]
Thus exact first-order stationarity, including vanishing smooth or limiting-subdifferential residual, does not imply any vanishing global objective gap for weakly convex objectives without additional geometry excluding nonoptimal stationary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly convex quartic has a nonoptimal point with zero stationarity residual and objective gap one, so stationarity alone cannot ensure global accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(0))=0\) but \(F(0)-F^\star=1\).

notation.meaning: limiting subdifferential, equal here to the gradient

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is directly checkable: the quartic is 4-weakly convex, zero is stationary, and its objective gap is one. The counterexample kind exactly fits the failure leaf, but the record has no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Expected Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covers stationarity certificates controlled in expectation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued random vector and \(S(X)\) is measurable and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[S(X)^q]\le\varepsilon^q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines expectation-based reporting for a nonnegative stationarity measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued random output, let \(S:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,+\infty]\) be measurable, and let \(q\ge1\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\). The assertion
\[
\mathbb{E}[S(X)^q]\le\varepsilon^q
\]
is an expected \((q,\varepsilon)\)-stationarity certificate. For \(q=1\), it bounds the expected residual. For \(q=2\), it bounds the second moment and implies \(\mathbb{E}[S(X)]\le\varepsilon\). The expectation is taken over all algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected certificate bounds a specified moment of a nonnegative measurable stationarity residual over all algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected Certificates

children.title: High-Confidence Certificates
children.top_down_role: Covers certificates holding at a prescribed confidence level.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Confidence Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a stationarity guarantee with an explicit failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a random output and \(S:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,+\infty]\) a measurable stationarity measure. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), the statement
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(S(X)\le\varepsilon\bigr)\ge1-\delta
\]
is an \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-high-confidence stationarity certificate. Equivalently, the bad event \(\{S(X)>\varepsilon\}\) has probability at most \(\delta\). The probability must be taken jointly over output selection, stochastic-oracle samples, validation samples, and any other algorithmic randomization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-confidence certificate bounds the stationarity residual except on an explicitly quantified failure event covering all algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(S(X)\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and probability statement match the High-Confidence Certificates leaf, and the good-event and bad-event formulations are equivalent. No source reference or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Expectation-to-Confidence Conversion
children.top_down_role: Covers mechanisms that convert average guarantees into confidence guarantees.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(Z\le\varepsilon\delta^{-1/q})\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the direct Markov conversion and its confidence-dependent tolerance loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\ge0\) be a random variable, and let \(q>0\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\delta\in(0,1)\). If \(\mathbb{E}[Z^q]\le\varepsilon^q\), then Markov's inequality gives
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(Z>\varepsilon\delta^{-1/q}\bigr)
\le
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Z^q]}{\varepsilon^q\delta^{-1}}
\le\delta.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(Z\le\varepsilon\delta^{-1/q}\bigr)\ge1-\delta,
\]
so an expected \(q\)-moment certificate yields an \((\varepsilon\delta^{-1/q},\delta)\)-high-confidence certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive expected-certificate tolerance, Markov's inequality converts a q-moment bound into confidence while enlarging the residual tolerance by delta to the power minus one over q.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-to-Confidence Conversion

children.title: Confidence Reporting Conventions
children.top_down_role: Covers the probability parameters and output events attached to certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Reporting Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes the interpretation of tolerances, failure events, and simultaneous claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A reported \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-certificate must identify the residual \(S\), its scaling convention, and the joint probability space, and must state
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(S(X)\le\varepsilon\bigr)\ge1-\delta.
\]
If \(m\) claims have failure events \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\) and assigned budgets \(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_m\), then simultaneous validity is reported using
\[
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{i=1}^m E_i^c\Bigr)
\ge1-\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_i.
\]
Independence must not be presumed unless explicitly established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Confidence reports must define the residual and probability space, include all randomness, and budget failure probabilities for simultaneous claims without silently assuming independence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\bigcap_{i=1}^m E_i^c)\ge1-\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_i\).

notation.meaning: failure event for the ith reported claim
failure budget assigned to the ith claim

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits a reporting-conventions leaf, and the simultaneous guarantee is the union bound without an independence assumption. The record needs an authoritative locator and should explicitly declare m as a positive integer and each failure budget as nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=x_R\) with \(\mathbb{P}(R=t\mid x_0,x5cldots,x_{T-1})=w_t/W\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects one computed iterate using prescribed nonnegative analysis weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\ge1\) be an integer. Given computed iterates \(x_0,\ldots,x_{T-1}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and deterministic weights \(w_0,\ldots,w_{T-1}\ge0\) with \(W:=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w_t>0\), draw an index \(R\), conditionally on the computed iterates, according to
\[
\mathbb{P}(R=t\mid x_0,\ldots,x_{T-1})=\frac{w_t}{W},
\qquad t=0,\ldots,T-1,
\]
and output \(X:=x_R\). For every measurable function \(S:\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,+\infty]\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[S(X)\mid x_0,\ldots,x_{T-1}]
=
\frac{1}{W}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w_tS(x_t).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample an iterate index in proportion to prescribed nonnegative weights and return that iterate; its conditional expected certificate equals the corresponding weighted average.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Iterate Output
Two-Phase Candidate Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates stochastic candidate generation from independent certificate validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix integers \(K,m\ge1\). In phase one, run the base stochastic method \(K\) times using independent randomness to produce candidates \(X_1,\ldots,X_K\). In phase two, for each candidate use a fresh validation sample \(V_k=(\zeta_{k,1},\ldots,\zeta_{k,m})\), independent of phase one and of the other validation samples, to compute an estimated residual \(\widehat S_k=\widehat S(X_k;V_k)\). Select
\[
\widehat k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le k\le K}\widehat S_k
\]
using a fixed tie-breaking rule, and output \(X_{\widehat k}\) together with \(\widehat S_{\widehat k}\) and the validation confidence parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent runs generate candidates; fresh samples estimate their residuals; the candidate with the smallest validated estimate is returned with its confidence metadata.
assumptions_latex: Validation samples are independent of candidate generation and mutually independent across candidates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_{\widehat k}\) is output for \(\widehat k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le k\le K}\widehat S_k\).

notation.meaning: validated residual estimate for candidate k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm template matches the Two-Phase Candidate Selection topic and correctly separates candidate generation from fresh validation. It supplies no theorem about the quality of the selected candidate, which is appropriate here, but it lacks a chapter-specific citation and locator.

children.title: Robust Certificate Estimators
children.top_down_role: Covers robust aggregation of noisy stationarity measurements.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Certificate Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a median-of-means deviation guarantee under finite variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m\) be independent copies of a scalar variable with mean \(\mu\) and variance at most \(\sigma^2\). Partition the samples into \(b\) equal blocks of size \(r=\lfloor m/b\rfloor\), discard any remainder, and let \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{MOM}}\) be the median of the block means. There exist universal constants \(c,C>0\) such that, whenever \(b\ge c\log(2/\delta)\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\left(
|\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{MOM}}-\mu|>
C\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{m}}
\right)
\le\delta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Median-of-means estimates a certificate mean with sub-Gaussian confidence scaling using only independence and a finite variance bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(|\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{MOM}}-\mu|>C\sigma\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/m})\le\delta\).

notation.meaning: median of the empirical block means

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated condition b at least a logarithmic lower bound is insufficient: allowing arbitrarily large b can make block size too small, and the claimed mean-deviation rate need not follow under finite variance alone. A valid median-of-means theorem needs a sourced block-count range or a specified logarithmic choice, together with delta and integer domains. Because this is a deviation theorem rather than a generic property, the content kind should also be theorem. An authoritative source is needed to fix the exact hypotheses and constants.

children.title: Candidate Validation
children.top_down_role: Covers independent assessment of candidate outputs.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a random candidate, \(V\) is validation data independent of the randomness used to generate \(X\), and \(S(X)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(U(X;V,\delta)\le\varepsilon<S(X))\le\delta\).

notation.meaning: upper confidence bound for the true residual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validates a candidate using an independent upper confidence bound for its residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a random candidate, let \(V\) be validation data independent of the randomness used to generate \(X\), and let \(S(X)\ge0\) be its true residual. For \(\delta\in(0,1)\), suppose that an estimator \(\widehat S(X;V)\) and a deterministic radius \(r(\delta)\ge0\) satisfy, conditionally on \(X\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(S(X)\le\widehat S(X;V)+r(\delta)\mid X\bigr)
\ge1-\delta
\]
almost surely. Define \(U(X;V,\delta):=\widehat S(X;V)+r(\delta)\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(U(X;V,\delta)\le\varepsilon<S(X)\bigr)
\le\delta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditionally valid upper confidence bound computed from fresh validation data limits the probability of accepting a candidate whose true residual exceeds the prescribed nonnegative tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Candidate Validation

children.title: Confidence Amplification
children.top_down_role: Covers repeated selection structures used to increase reliability.

assumptions_latex: \(K\ge1\) is an integer and \(B_1,\ldots,B_K\) are independent Bernoulli random variables.
The aggregation is valid whenever \(\sum_{k=1}^K B_k>K/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\text{aggregate invalid})\le\exp(-2K(p-1/2)^2)\).

notation.meaning: lower bound on single-run success probability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amplifies a constant-success certificate by independent repetition and majority aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\ge1\) be an integer, and let \(B_1,\ldots,B_K\in\{0,1\}\) be independent random variables such that \(\mathbb{P}(B_k=1)\ge p>1/2\) for every \(k\). If an aggregation rule returns a valid output whenever \(\sum_{k=1}^K B_k>K/2\), then Hoeffding's inequality gives
\[
\mathbb{P}(\text{aggregate invalid})
\le
\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{k=1}^K B_k\le\frac{K}{2}\right)
\le
\exp\bigl(-2K(p-1/2)^2\bigr).
\]
Therefore, for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\), choosing
\[
K\ge\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2(p-1/2)^2}
\]
makes the aggregate failure probability at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition and an aggregation rule that succeeds under a strict valid majority reduce the failure probability exponentially; a logarithmic number of repetitions achieves any specified confidence level.
knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Amplification

children.title: Validation Contamination Limits
children.top_down_role: Covers failure when validation samples or estimates are insufficiently reliable.

assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) are sampled from \((1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon Q\), where \(P,Q\) are arbitrary distributions on \([0,1]\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\widehat\theta}\sup_{P,Q}\mathbb{E}|\widehat\theta-\mathbb{E}_P Z|\geq \varepsilon/(2(1-\varepsilon))\).

notation.meaning: estimator of the uncontaminated validation mean

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic limit for scalar validation under adversarial Huber contamination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_0=\delta_0\), \(Q_0=\delta_1\), \(P_1=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon))\), and \(Q_1=\delta_0\). The contaminated laws \((1-\varepsilon)P_0+\varepsilon Q_0\) and \((1-\varepsilon)P_1+\varepsilon Q_1\) coincide, while their uncontaminated means differ by \(\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)\). Consequently, for every sample size \(n\) and every estimator \(\widehat\theta(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\),
\[
\max_{i\in\{0,1\}}\mathbb{E}_i\left|\widehat\theta-\mathbb{E}_{P_i}Z\right|\geq \frac{\varepsilon}{2(1-\varepsilon)}.
\]
Thus validation alone cannot certify accuracy below the contamination scale without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under arbitrary epsilon-contamination, two clean validation laws with different means can generate identical observations, forcing estimation error proportional to epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation Contamination Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-point contamination construction and failure-boundary content kind fit the leaf, but the nontrivial minimax lower bound has no cited source or inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: \(G(x,\xi)\) is measurable and satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial f(x)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\xi_k)\), with output \(x_R\) or a prescribed average.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Euclidean stochastic subgradient iteration with explicit output conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a horizon \(K\geq1\), positive stepsizes \(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{K-1}\), and conditionally independent oracle samples \(\xi_k\), compute
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\xi_k),\qquad k=0,\ldots,K-1.
\]
A last-iterate implementation returns \(x_K\). An averaged implementation returns \(\bar x_K=(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k)\). For nonconvex or weakly convex analysis, a randomized implementation may instead draw \(R\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\) from a distribution fixed by the analysis and return \(x_R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an initial point, repeatedly move opposite an unbiased stochastic subgradient and return the last, averaged, or randomly selected iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Stochastic Subgradient Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the basic stochastic-subgradient leaf, but no source is cited. The assumptions also contain the malformed range `k=0,ldots,K-1`, which should use `\ldots`.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\xi_k))\in X\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projected method for closed convex constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in X\), a horizon \(K\geq1\), stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\), and oracle samples \(\xi_k\), set
\[
x_{k+1}=\Pi_X\bigl(x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\xi_k)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,K-1,
\]
where \(\Pi_X(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in X}\|y-z\|^2\). Every iterate is feasible. The method returns \(x_K\), a weighted average of \(x_0,\ldots,x_{K-1}\), or a randomized iterate \(x_R\), according to the stationarity or objective criterion being evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each stochastic subgradient step is projected onto the closed convex feasible set, so all iterates remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Stochastic Subgradient Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected update is mathematically standard and the algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative citation or locator.

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\) admits an unbiased stochastic subgradient oracle \(G\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha_kr}(x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\xi_k))\).

notation.meaning: stochastic subgradient of the loss term

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite stochastic subgradient method with a convex proximable regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the composite objective \(f+r\), initialize \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}r\). At iteration \(k\), sample \(\xi_k\), evaluate \(G_k=G(x_k,\xi_k)\), and compute
\[
x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{r(y)+\langle G_k,y-x_k\rangle+\frac{1}{2\alpha_k}\|y-x_k\|^2\right\}
=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha_kr}(x_k-\alpha_kG_k).
\]
After \(K\) iterations, return \(x_K\), a prescribed average, or a randomized iterate \(x_R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic subgradient step for the loss is followed implicitly by the proximal mapping of a convex regularizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Stochastic Subgradient Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composite proximal stochastic-subgradient update is internally consistent and correctly classified as an algorithm, but it has no supporting citation.

assumptions_latex: \(F(\cdot,\xi)\) is proper and lower semicontinuous almost surely
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\{F(y,\xi_k)+\|y-x_k\|^2/(2\alpha_k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact samplewise proximal-point update for weakly convex losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stepsizes \(0<\alpha_k<1/\rho\), and samples \(\xi_k\), compute
\[
x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{F(y,\xi_k)+\frac{1}{2\alpha_k}\|y-x_k\|^2\right\},
\qquad k=0,\ldots,K-1.
\]
The stepsize restriction makes each sample subproblem strongly convex when the common weak-convexity bound holds, hence its minimizer is unique. After the prescribed horizon, return \(x_K\) or a randomized iterate \(x_R\) selected according to the stationarity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, minimize one sampled weakly convex loss plus a quadratic centered at the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Proximal-Point Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The samplewise proximal-point update and weak-convexity stepsize restriction fit the leaf, but the uniqueness assertion and algorithm formulation require a cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\{F(x_k,\xi_k)+\langle g_k,y-x_k\rangle+r(y)+\|y-x_k\|^2/(2\alpha_k)\}\).

notation.meaning: sample subgradient at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine sample-model update with optional convex regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}r\). After sampling \(\xi_k\), choose \(g_k\in\partial F(x_k,\xi_k)\) and form the affine model \(m_k(y)=F(x_k,\xi_k)+\langle g_k,y-x_k\rangle\). Compute
\[
x_{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{m_k(y)+r(y)+\frac{1}{2\alpha_k}\|y-x_k\|^2\right\}.
\]
Repeat for \(k=0,\ldots,K-1\), then return the last iterate, a specified average, or a randomized iterate. The constant term in \(m_k\) may be omitted computationally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize the sampled loss at the current point, add the regularizer and a quadratic stabilization term, and minimize the resulting model.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Linearized-Model Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine sample-model algorithm fits the container, but no source is provided and the intended subdifferential for the potentially nonsmooth sample loss is not specified.

assumptions_latex: \(c(\cdot,\xi)\) is differentiable at each queried point
\(\alpha_k>0\) and the displayed subproblem has a minimizer
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\{h(c(x_k,\xi_k)+\nabla c(x_k,\xi_k)(y-x_k),\xi_k)+\|y-x_k\|^2/(2\alpha_k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Samplewise prox-linear update for convex-composite stochastic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), sample \(\xi_k\) and replace the inner mapping by its first-order expansion at \(x_k\). Compute
\[
x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{h\bigl(c(x_k,\xi_k)+\nabla c(x_k,\xi_k)(y-x_k),\xi_k\bigr)+\frac{1}{2\alpha_k}\|y-x_k\|^2\right\}.
\]
Iterate for \(k=0,\ldots,K-1\). The output is \(x_K\) or a randomized iterate \(x_R\), as specified by the desired expected-stationarity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize the smooth inner mapping of a sampled convex-composite loss, retain the outer convex function, and solve the regularized model.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Prox-Linear Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The samplewise convex-composite prox-linear update fits the algorithm leaf, but no authoritative source or inspectable locator supports the stated formulation and output convention.

assumptions_latex: \(\lambda_k>0\) and each model subproblem is solvable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\{\tfrac12\|R(x_k,\xi_k)+J_R(x_k,\xi_k)(y-x_k)\|^2+\tfrac{\lambda_k}{2}\|y-x_k\|^2\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized samplewise Gauss-Newton update for nonlinear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). At iteration \(k\), sample \(\xi_k\), evaluate \(R_k=R(x_k,\xi_k)\) and \(J_k=J_R(x_k,\xi_k)\), and compute
\[
x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{\frac12\|R_k+J_k(y-x_k)\|^2+\frac{\lambda_k}{2}\|y-x_k\|^2\right\}.
\]
After \(K\) updates, return \(x_K\) or a prescribed randomized iterate. The positive regularizer controls ill-conditioning and selects a unique step when the quadratic model is otherwise singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize a sampled residual, minimize its squared norm with positive quadratic regularization, and return the resulting iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Stochastic Gauss–Newton Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regularized samplewise Gauss–Newton update is coherent and correctly classified as an algorithm, but it lacks any supporting citation.

assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and strictly convex on an open convex set containing the iterates
\(m_{x_k}(\cdot,\xi_k)\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous sample model
\(\alpha_k>0\) and the subproblem has a minimizer
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\{m_{x_k}(y,\xi_k)+D_h(y,x_k)/\alpha_k\}\).

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the kernel
sample model based at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-Euclidean stochastic model update generated by a Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\). Given \(x_0\) in the interior of the kernel domain, sample \(\xi_k\), construct the model \(m_{x_k}(\cdot,\xi_k)\), and compute
\[
x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\left\{m_{x_k}(y,\xi_k)+\frac{1}{\alpha_k}D_h(y,x_k)\right\}.
\]
The minimization domain is the intersection of the model and kernel domains. Repeat for the prescribed horizon and return \(x_K\), an average defined in primal or dual coordinates, or a randomized iterate specified in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize each stochastic local model with a Bregman divergence penalty, allowing geometry adapted to the objective or feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Stochastic Model Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bregman model update fits the leaf, but it has no source. The kernel assumptions also do not fully specify the domain and differentiability conditions normally needed for every displayed divergence and iterate.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\) approximately minimizes \(f(y)+\|y-x_t\|^2/(2\lambda)\), a strongly convex proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer proximal construction for a weakly convex population objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At outer iteration \(t\), define
\[
q_t(y)=f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x_t\|^2.
\]
Because \(\lambda<1/\rho\), the function \(q_t\) is \((1/\lambda-\rho)\)-strongly convex. Invoke a stochastic inner solver to produce \(x_{t+1}\) satisfying a prescribed expected objective-gap, distance, or subgradient residual tolerance for \(q_t\). Continue for \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), then return the final center \(x_T\) or a randomized center \(x_R\) chosen according to the outer stationarity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each outer step approximately solves a strongly convex proximal regularization of the weakly convex population objective around the current center.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Proximal Guidance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outer proximal-guidance construction and algorithm kind fit the container, but no source is cited and the required approximation criterion is left as a menu rather than fixed algorithm data.

assumptions_latex: \(G(y,\xi)\) is an unbiased stochastic subgradient of \(f\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_{j+1}=y_j-eta_{t,j}(G(y_j,\xi_{t,j})+(y_j-x_t)/\lambda)\) approximately solves the outer subproblem.

notation.meaning: proximal subproblem at outer stage t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic subgradient inner solver for an outer proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed outer center \(x_t\), initialize \(y_0=x_t\). For \(j=0,\ldots,J_t-1\), independently sample \(\xi_{t,j}\) and update
\[
y_{j+1}=y_j-\eta_{t,j}\left(G(y_j,\xi_{t,j})+\frac{1}{\lambda}(y_j-x_t)\right).
\]
The term in parentheses is an unbiased stochastic subgradient of \(q_t\). Return either \(y_{J_t}\) or the weighted average \(\bar y_t=(\sum_{j=0}^{J_t-1}\eta_{t,j}y_j)/(\sum_{j=0}^{J_t-1}\eta_{t,j})\) as the approximate proximal point \(x_{t+1}\), using the convention fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic subgradient solver targets each strongly convex proximal subproblem and returns its last or weighted-average inner iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Inner-Subproblem Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inner stochastic-subgradient solver fits the leaf, but no source is provided. The conclusion writes `eta_{t,j}` instead of the introduced `\eta_{t,j}`, making that formula notationally inconsistent.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex
\(w_s>0\) and each stage solver has a prescribed finite budget
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{s+1}\approx\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda_s f}(x_s)\), and the reported center is sampled with probability proportional to \(w_s\).

notation.meaning: center at the beginning of stage s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-stage proximal guidance with randomized stage selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an initial center \(x_0\), stage count \(S\), parameters \(0<\lambda_s<1/\rho\), inner budgets \(J_s\), and weights \(w_s>0\). At stage \(s\), approximately minimize
\[
q_s(y)=f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda_s}\|y-x_s\|^2
\]
with \(J_s\) stochastic inner iterations, and set the returned approximate minimizer as \(x_{s+1}\). After all stages, draw \(R\in\{0,\ldots,S-1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(R=s)=w_s/(\sum_{i=0}^{S-1}w_i)\) and output \(x_R\), or output \(x_S\) when a last-stage guarantee is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a budgeted stochastic proximal solve at each stage, update the center, and report either the final or a weighted-random stage center.
knowledge_statements.title: Stagewise Proximal Guidance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The staged proximal-guidance scheme is appropriately classified as an algorithm, but it lacks a citation and does not define the accuracy condition represented by approximate minimization.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
The proximal parameter satisfies \(0<\lambda<\rho^{-1}\), and an inner stochastic solver can approximately minimize each proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned candidate is selected using an independently computed proximal-stationarity estimate.

notation.meaning: candidate centers produced in phase one

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic candidate-generation and independent-selection form; precise published variants differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}F\), phase one generates candidates \(x_1,\ldots,x_M\) by approximately solving successive problems \(\min_y Q_\lambda(y;x_{j-1})\) with fresh stochastic oracle samples. In phase two, use samples independent of phase one to compute approximate proximal points \(\widehat y_j\approx\arg\min_y Q_\lambda(y;x_j)\) and estimates \(\widehat G_j=\lambda^{-1}(x_j-\widehat y_j)\). Return \(x_{j_*}\), where \(j_*\in\arg\min_{1\le j\le M}\lVert\widehat G_j\rVert\). Inner sample sizes and stopping tolerances are prescribed inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate several candidates by stochastic proximal subproblems, independently estimate each candidate's proximal stationarity, and return the candidate with the smallest estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Phase Proximally Guided Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited for this particular two-phase algorithm, its independent selection phase, or the required inner accuracies. Published variants differ materially, so the stated algorithm cannot be validated as written.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally integrable and bounded below.
\(U\) has a specified smoothing distribution, and \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method optimizes \(f_\mu\) using function-value estimators of \(\nabla f_\mu\) whenever the smoothing identity is valid.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-neutral smoothing representation; gradient estimators depend on the chosen law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the random smoothing \(f_\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu U)]\). For Gaussian smoothing with \(U\sim N(0,I_d)\), whenever differentiation under the expectation is justified, \[\nabla f_\mu(x)=\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[f(x+\mu U)U]=\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}[(f(x+\mu U)-f(x))U].\] A random-smoothing method forms an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the applicable right-hand side and applies a stochastic update to \(f_\mu\), optionally projecting onto the feasible set. The radius \(\mu\) controls smoothing bias and estimator variability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random perturbations define a smooth surrogate whose gradient can, under suitable conditions, be estimated from function values and used in stochastic updates.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Smoothing Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian smoothing identity requires precise integrability and differentiation hypotheses not supplied here. A source is also needed to establish whether this method leaf should contain an algorithm rather than the current representation-plus-update description.

assumptions_latex: Only one noisy function value is available per iteration.
\(U_k\sim N(0,I_d)\), and the observation satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[Y_k\mid x_k,U_k]=f(x_k+\mu_kU_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditionally on \(x_k\), \(g_k\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\nabla f_{\mu_k}(x_k)\) under the Gaussian smoothing identity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian one-point feedback with one fresh function observation per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in X\), stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\), and radii \(\mu_k>0\). At iteration \(k\), draw \(U_k\sim N(0,I_d)\), observe only \(Y_k\) at \(x_k+\mu_kU_k\), set \(g_k=\mu_k^{-1}Y_kU_k\), and update \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname{proj}_X(x_k-\alpha_kg_k).\] After \(T\) iterations, return a prescribed last, averaged, or randomly selected iterate. With the stated conditional-mean model and valid Gaussian smoothing identity, \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f_{\mu_k}(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration uses one perturbed noisy function value to estimate the smoothed gradient, then takes a projected stochastic step.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Point Feedback Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional unbiasedness claim requires integrability conditions, and the last/averaged/random output alternatives are not one fully specified algorithm. No source identifies the intended one-point weakly convex variant.

assumptions_latex: Two function values using the same random direction and coupled observation noise are available per iteration.
\(U_k\sim N(0,I_d)\), and the paired difference is conditionally unbiased for the corresponding objective difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditionally on \(x_k\), the paired estimator targets \(\nabla f_{\mu_k}(x_k)\) and cancels any common additive offset.

notation.meaning: paired function observations at the base and perturbed points

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward two-point Gaussian estimator; symmetric variants require a separate formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_0\in X\), \(\alpha_k>0\), and \(\mu_k>0\). Draw \(U_k\sim N(0,I_d)\), obtain paired observations \(Y_k^0\) at \(x_k\) and \(Y_k^+\) at \(x_k+\mu_kU_k\), and form \(g_k=\mu_k^{-1}(Y_k^+-Y_k^0)U_k\). Update \[x_{k+1}=\operatorname{proj}_X(x_k-\alpha_kg_k).\] Return a prescribed iterate after \(T\) steps. If \(\mathbb{E}[Y_k^+-Y_k^0\mid x_k,U_k]=f(x_k+\mu_kU_k)-f(x_k)\), then \(\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f_{\mu_k}(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A paired base-point and perturbed evaluation yields a difference estimator for the smoothed gradient and removes common additive offsets.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Point Feedback Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paired-difference identity is plausible but needs integrability and a cited observation model. The unspecified output rule and absence of a source prevent validation of the exact two-point algorithm.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Stochastic Optimization over Proximally Smooth Sets

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a smooth Riemannian manifold equipped with a retraction \(R\).
The stochastic oracle returns \(v_k\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\) with a prescribed conditional model or subgradient property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iterate remains on \(\mathcal M\), and the tangent stochastic step is transferred to the manifold through \(R\).

notation.meaning: retraction from the tangent bundle to the manifold

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic manifold-constrained stochastic update using a first-order retraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in\mathcal M\). For \(k=0,\ldots,T-1\), sample the stochastic oracle, construct a tangent direction \(v_k\in T_{x_k}\mathcal M\), choose \(\alpha_k>0\), and set \[x_{k+1}=R_{x_k}(-\alpha_kv_k).\] The retraction must satisfy \(R_x(0_x)=x\) and \(D R_x(0_x)=\operatorname{id}_{T_x\mathcal M}\). The output is a prescribed last or randomly selected iterate. Thus feasibility with respect to \(\mathcal M\) is exact even though the objective model and direction are stochastic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct a stochastic direction in the current tangent space and retract the tangent step back to the constraint manifold.
knowledge_statements.title: Retraction-Based Stochastic Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle property is left as an alternative rather than a precise assumption, and the retraction must be defined at every attempted tangent step for the feasibility conclusion. No source supports the intended stochastic nonsmooth manifold method.

children.title: Objective Model Construction
children.top_down_role: Covers stochastic local models for the objective component.

assumptions_latex: For almost every sample \(\xi\), the realization \(f(\cdot,\xi)\) admits a stochastic subgradient at the base point \(x\).
A model curvature parameter \(\gamma\ge 0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model agrees with the sampled objective at \(x\) and provides a regularized first-order prediction away from \(x\).

notation.meaning: sampled objective model at base point x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically regularized stochastic first-order objective model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a base point \(x\) and sample \(\xi\), choose \(g(x,\xi)\in\partial f(x,\xi)\) and define \[m_f(y;x,\xi)=f(x,\xi)+\langle g(x,\xi),y-x\rangle+\frac{\gamma}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2.\] Then \(m_f(x;x,\xi)=f(x,xi)\), and the linear part records sampled first-order information. For a \(\rho\)-weakly convex realization, choosing \(\gamma\ge\rho\) yields a convex quadratic model. Batch models replace the displayed quantities by sample averages while preserving base-point agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize a sampled weakly convex objective at the current point and add enough quadratic curvature to obtain a tractable local model.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Model Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subdifferential notion and model-accuracy framework are unspecified and uncited. The displayed base-point identity also contains the inconsistent expression f(x,xi) instead of f(x,\xi).

children.title: Constraint Model Construction
children.top_down_role: Covers local models for constraint geometry or violation.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is described by \(c_j(y)\le 0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\).
Each sampled constraint realization admits a subgradient at the base point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model constraints match sampled constraint values at \(x\) and define a tractable local feasible region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic local models for inequality constraints; conservatism requires additional error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(j\), base point \(x\), and sample \(\zeta\), choose \(a_j(x,\zeta)\in\partial c_j(x,\zeta)\) and define \[m_{c_j}(y;x,\zeta)=c_j(x,\zeta)+\langle a_j(x,\zeta),y-x\rangle+\frac{\tau_j}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2.\] The modeled feasible set is \(C_x(\zeta)=\{y:m_{c_j}(y;x,\zeta)\le0\ \text{for all }j\}\). Base-point agreement \(m_{c_j}(x;x,\zeta)=c_j(x,\zeta)\) holds. A positive \(\tau_j\) supplies curvature but does not alone guarantee that \(C_x(\zeta)\) is an inner approximation of the true feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model every sampled inequality by a subgradient linearization plus curvature, then intersect the modeled inequalities to form the local feasible region.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Model Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assumptions first describe deterministic constraints c_j(y) but the construction uses sampled realizations c_j(x,\zeta). A source and a precise stochastic constraint model are required before the representation can be validated.

children.title: Coupled Model Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Covers subproblems that combine objective and constraint surrogates.

assumptions_latex: An objective model \(m_f(\cdot;x,\xi)\) and constraint models \(m_{c_j}(\cdot;x,\zeta)\) are available at \(x\).
The regularization parameter satisfies \(\beta>0\), and the modeled feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any minimizer jointly balances objective prediction, proximity to \(x\), and satisfaction of every modeled constraint.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard-constraint coupled proximal model with an optional exact-penalty restoration form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At base point \(x\), solve \[y_x\in\arg\min_y\left\{m_f(y;x,\xi)+\frac{\beta}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2:m_{c_j}(y;x,\zeta)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,q\right\}.\] If the modeled constraints may be inconsistent, introduce \(s\ge0\) and instead minimize \(m_f(y;x,\xi)+\frac{\beta}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2+\kappa\lVert s\rVert_1\) subject to \(m_{c_j}(y;x,\zeta)\le s_j\). Set the next iterate to \(y_x\), or accept it through a prescribed feasibility test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jointly minimize the local objective model and proximal regularizer while enforcing all local constraint models, optionally using penalized slacks for restoration.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Model Subproblems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends a hard-constrained subproblem, a slack-penalty restoration variant, and an unspecified feasibility acceptance test. The penalty parameter \kappa is not introduced, and no source selects or supports one complete coupled-model algorithm.

children.title: Model Compatibility Failures
children.top_down_role: Covers mismatches between objective models and constraint models.

assumptions_latex: Only base-point value agreement is imposed on a constraint model.
The true scalar constraint is \(c(y)=-y\le0\) at the feasible base point \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Base-point agreement alone neither preserves feasible directions nor ensures useful coupled-model steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure showing that value consistency is weaker than first-order model compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the true problem be \(\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}}-y\) subject to \(c(y)=-y\le0\), and take \(x=0\). Define \(m_f(y;0)=-y\) and \(m_c(y;0)=y^2\). Although \(m_c(0;0)=c(0)=0\), the modeled constraint \(m_c(y;0)\le0\) permits only \(y=0\), whereas the true constraint permits every \(y\ge0\). Consequently, for every \(\beta>0\), the coupled proximal model has the unique feasible solution \(y=0\), despite the existence of feasible objective-decreasing directions. The missing requirement is first-order constraint-model accuracy or directional compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint model can match the true value at the base point yet eliminate every genuinely feasible descent direction, causing complete stagnation.
knowledge_statements.title: Model Compatibility Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The numerical counterexample is internally correct and the counterexample kind fits the failure leaf, but the asserted missing compatibility requirement is framework-dependent and has no cited source or inspectable locator.

assumptions_latex: The stochastic approximation uses nonnegative stepsizes \((\alpha_k)\).
Oracle errors have bounded conditional second moments and the usual martingale-difference structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule has infinite cumulative travel but finite cumulative squared noise weight.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Robbins-Monro diminishing-step conditions, stated independently of a particular weakly convex method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A diminishing schedule satisfies \[\alpha_k>0,\qquad \alpha_k\to0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2<\infty.\] A standard power-law instance is \(\alpha_k=a(k+b)^{-p}\), where \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and \(p\in(1/2,1]\). The divergent first sum prevents the method from exhausting its total movement prematurely, while square summability controls accumulated stochastic variance. Additional restrictions on proximal or model curvature remain algorithm dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use positive steps that vanish, have a divergent sum, and have a convergent squared sum; power laws with exponent above one half are standard.
knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing Schedules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The summability conditions and power-law range are mathematically standard, and the condition kind fits the schedule leaf. Nevertheless, no citation or locator supports the stochastic-approximation interpretation or its applicability in this chapter.

assumptions_latex: A finite iteration horizon \(T\ge1\) is fixed before execution.
The relevant error estimate has competing terms proportional to \((T\alpha)^{-1}\) and \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choosing \(\alpha_T\) proportional to \(T^{-1/2}\) balances the two terms at order \(T^{-1/2}\).

notation.meaning: constant stepsize used through the horizon

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic finite-horizon balancing rule, not a universal convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a stationarity or model-error estimate after \(T\) iterations has the form \[B_T(\alpha)\le \frac{A}{T\alpha}+C\alpha,\] where \(A,C>0\) do not depend on \(T\) or \(\alpha\). The minimizing constant choice is \(\alpha_T=\sqrt{A/(CT)}\), giving \(B_T(\alpha_T)\le2\sqrt{AC/T}\). More generally, \(\alpha_T=\Theta(T^{-1/2})\) balances optimization progress against stochastic variability. Any smoothing radius, inner tolerance, or proximal parameter must be tuned simultaneously when it contributes additional terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a known horizon, choose a constant step proportional to the inverse square root of the horizon when progress and noise terms have reciprocal forms.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Tuned Schedules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic balancing rule is correct under the displayed generic bound, and the principle kind fits the leaf. A source is still required for the bound and its relevance to the intended stochastic weakly convex method family.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(k\), a model \(m_k\), a trial step \(s_k\), and an observed merit value are available.
The regularization parameters are bounded below by \(\sigma_{\min}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful steps reduce regularization, while unsuccessful or unreliable steps increase it and reject the trial point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-ratio-style adaptive quadratic regularization for stochastic local models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_k\) and \(\sigma_k\ge\sigma_{\min}\), compute a trial step by approximately minimizing \(m_k(x_k+s)+(\sigma_k/2)\lVert s\rVert^2\). Using sufficiently accurate, preferably independent, estimates, form \[r_k=\frac{\text{observed merit decrease}}{\text{predicted regularized-model decrease}}.\] For fixed \(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\), accept \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when \(r_k\ge\eta_1\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). Decrease \(\sigma_k\) when \(r_k\ge\eta_2\), retain it for intermediate ratios, and increase it when \(r_k<\eta_1\), always enforcing \(\sigma_{k+1}\ge\sigma_{\min}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adapt model regularization using observed versus predicted decrease: accept reliable steps and weaken regularization, but reject unreliable steps and strengthen it.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Regularization Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Observed merit, predicted decrease, update factors, denominator safeguards, and stochastic accuracy requirements are not defined. Without a cited adaptive-regularization variant, this is not a reproducible algorithm for the exact leaf.
