knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Subgradient Rate Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Moreau-envelope rate for stochastic subgradient iterates on weakly convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex. Suppose an unbiased stochastic subgradient oracle has uniformly bounded second moment \(L^2\). For \(\lambda<1/\rho\), run stochastic subgradient iterations for \(T\) steps with stepsizes of order \(T^{-1/2}\), and select \(x_R\) with probability proportional to the stepsizes. The standard envelope-descent estimate has the form \[\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_R)\|^2\leq \frac{C(\Delta+L^2)}{\sqrt{T}},\] where \(\Delta=f_\lambda(x_0)-\inf f\) and \(C\) depends on \(\rho\) and \(\lambda\). Consequently, achieving \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_R)\|\leq\varepsilon\) requires \(T=O(\varepsilon^{-4})\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic subgradient descent attains squared envelope-stationarity of order T^{-1/2}, corresponding to order ε^{-4} oracle complexity for expected envelope-gradient norm ε.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
The oracle satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[g(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial f(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}\|g(x,\xi)\|^2\leq L^2\).
\(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), and the sampling rule is proportional to the iteration stepsizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_R)\|^2=O(T^{-1/2})\), hence \(T=O(\varepsilon^{-4})\) suffices for \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_R)\|\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Moreau envelope of f with parameter λ

review_flags: Exact stochastic weakly convex subgradient theorem and constants require an authoritative source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the rate-family leaf, and the stated T^{-1/2} squared-envelope rate and epsilon^{-4} expected-norm scale are plausible. However, the precise oracle assumptions, stepsize rule, output distribution, and dependence on rho and lambda require an inspectable theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Based Rate Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected envelope-stationarity rate for stochastic one-sided model minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x,\xi)]\) be \(\rho\)-weakly convex and bounded below. At iteration \(t\), let \(f_{x_t}(\cdot,\xi_t)\) be a stochastic model that is convex up to a fixed quadratic, agrees with the sampled loss at \(x_t\), and underestimates it up to a quadratic error. Define \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_y\left\{f_{x_t}(y,\xi_t)+\frac{1}{2\alpha_t}\|y-x_t\|^2\right\}.\] Under a uniform second-moment bound on model slopes, stepsizes \(\alpha_t\asymp T^{-1/2}\), and stepsize-proportional output sampling, the model-based descent inequality yields \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_R)\|^2=O(T^{-1/2})\). Thus the corresponding expected-norm oracle complexity is \(O(\varepsilon^{-4})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratically regularized stochastic model minimization has the canonical T^{-1/2} squared envelope-gradient rate and ε^{-4} expected-norm complexity.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic models satisfy consistency and a uniform quadratic one-sided approximation bound.
Model slopes have uniformly bounded conditional second moment.
The envelope parameter and proximal stepsizes dominate the weak-convexity and model-error moduli.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_R)\|^2=O(T^{-1/2})\) and the expected-norm complexity is \(O(\varepsilon^{-4})\).

notation.meaning: stochastic local model at base point x
Moreau envelope of the population objective

review_flags: The precise model axioms, admissible parameters, and rate constants require a model-based stochastic optimization source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits this rate-family leaf, but the one-sided model conditions and admissible parameter relations are only described informally. An algorithm-specific theorem source is needed to determine whether these hypotheses support the asserted rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Guidance Rate Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer–inner complexity template for proximally guided stochastic weakly convex optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex. Choose \(\gamma<1/\rho\). At outer iterate \(x_s\), approximately minimize the strongly convex function \[y\mapsto f(y)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|y-x_s\|^2\] by a stochastic inner method, and let \(x_{s+1}\) be its approximate minimizer. If the conditional inner error is summable or allocated so that its aggregate contribution is at most the outer descent term, then a uniformly sampled outer iterate \(x_R\) satisfies \[\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\gamma(x_R)\|^2\leq O(S^{-1/2}).\] With the usual accuracy schedule for stochastic strongly convex subproblems, the total stochastic-oracle cost for \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\gamma(x_R)\|\leq\varepsilon\) is of order \(\varepsilon^{-4}\), up to logarithmic factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal guidance reduces weakly convex stationarity to stochastic strongly convex subproblems, yielding the standard ε^{-4} oracle scale under controlled inner errors.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
\(0<\gamma<1/\rho\), so every guided subproblem is strongly convex.
Conditional inner-solve errors obey the prescribed summable or accuracy-allocation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical guided scheme attains \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f_\gamma(x_R)\|^2=O(S^{-1/2})\) with total stochastic-oracle complexity \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-4})\).
review_flags: Different proximal-guidance schemes have distinct inner schedules and logarithmic factors; an exact theorem source is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but the outer rate, inner accuracy allocation, total oracle cost, and logarithmic factors vary among proximal-guidance schemes. The generic inner-error condition is insufficient to validate the displayed rate without an exact theorem source.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Free Rate Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothed envelope-stationarity template for zeroth-order stochastic estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, and let function values be observed through an unbiased stochastic oracle. Form a two-point randomized estimator \[G_\mu(x;u,\xi)=\frac{d}{2\mu}\bigl(F(x+\mu u,\xi)-F(x-\mu u,\xi)\bigr)u,\] where \(u\) is uniform on the unit sphere. Applying a stochastic weakly convex method to the smoothed objective \(f_\mu\) yields a generic decomposition \[\mathbb{E}\|\nabla (f_\mu)_\lambda(x_R)\|^2\leq \frac{C_1(d)}{\sqrt{T}}+C_2\mu^2.\] Therefore \(T\) and \(\mu\) must jointly control sampling error and smoothing bias; dimension-dependent constants distinguish derivative-free rates from first-order rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeroth-order rates combine a dimension-dependent stochastic term with smoothing bias, so iteration count and smoothing radius must be chosen jointly.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is Lipschitz, bounded below, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
Function-value noise permits a conditionally unbiased two-point estimator with bounded second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla (f_\mu)_\lambda(x_R)\|^2\leq C_1(d)T^{-1/2}+C_2\mu^2\) under the stated estimator model.

notation.meaning: uniform random direction on the unit sphere

review_flags: The smoothing-bias power and dimension factor depend on the oracle, smoothing law, and regularity assumptions.
A derivative-free weakly convex rate theorem is required before promotion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the derivative-free rate-family leaf. The dimension factor, estimator second moment, preservation of weak convexity under smoothing, and mu-squared bias term depend on the smoothing and noise models, so the displayed decomposition cannot be validated without a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected Moreau-envelope stationarity as the baseline stochastic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a random output \(X\) of a stochastic method applied to a \(\rho\)-weakly convex objective \(f\), fix \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\) and define the stationarity residual \(Z=\|\nabla f_\lambda(X)\|\). An expected squared-stationarity guarantee is \[\mathbb{E}[Z^2]\leq\varepsilon^2.\] It immediately implies \(\mathbb{E}[Z]\leq\varepsilon\) by the second-moment inequality. The guarantee averages over every source of algorithmic and oracle randomness; it does not assert that each realization is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary, nor does it alone prescribe a small failure probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation guarantee bounds the mean squared envelope-gradient residual over all randomness; it is weaker than a specified high-probability guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The random residual \(Z=\|\nabla f_\lambda(X)\|\) is square-integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[Z^2]\leq\varepsilon^2\) implies \(\mathbb{E}[Z]\leq\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard second-moment formulation and follows directly from the L2-to-L1 inequality.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Confidence Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an expected squared residual into a fixed-success-probability statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=\|\nabla f_\lambda(X)\|\geq0\) be the stationarity residual of a random output. If \(\mathbb{E}[Z^2]\leq\varepsilon^2\), then for every fixed \(c>1\), \[\mathbb{P}(Z\leq c\varepsilon)\geq 1-c^{-2}.\] In particular, \(c=\sqrt{2}\) gives success probability at least \(1/2\). Thus an expected squared-residual rate yields a constant-confidence stationarity guarantee without additional tail assumptions, at the cost of a constant-factor relaxation of the target residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mean-square residual bound gives constant success probability through Markov’s inequality, with only a constant-factor relaxation in stationarity tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(c>1\), \(\mathbb{P}(Z\leq c\varepsilon)\geq1-c^{-2}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Direct application of Markov's inequality to the nonnegative variable Z squared.

knowledge_statements.title: Concentration-Based High-Confidence Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct high-probability stationarity under sub-Gaussian or bounded stochastic errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a stochastic weakly convex method admits a martingale decomposition for its squared envelope-stationarity residual, with conditionally sub-Gaussian increments of variance proxy \(\sigma^2\) and uniformly bounded predictable terms. Then a concentration argument yields a bound of the generic form \[\|\nabla f_\lambda(X_T)\|^2\leq \frac{C_0}{\sqrt{T}}+C_1\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{T}}+C_2\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{T}\] with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Consequently, confidence enters logarithmically rather than through the reciprocal factor produced by a direct Markov conversion. The constants and exact powers depend on the algorithm's descent inequality and noise model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under suitable martingale-tail assumptions, direct concentration yields high-probability envelope-stationarity with logarithmic dependence on inverse failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The algorithmic error has an adapted martingale-difference decomposition.
The increments are conditionally sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(\sigma^2\) and satisfy the required boundedness conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent repetition converts constant success probability into arbitrary confidence when successful candidates can be selected reliably.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a nonnegative stationarity residual and suppose each independent run returns a candidate \(X_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(Z(X_k)\leq\varepsilon)\geq p\) for some \(p\in(0,1)\). Run the method independently \(K\) times and apply a selection procedure that returns a successful candidate whenever at least one run is successful. Then \[\mathbb{P}\!\left(\min_{1\leq k\leq K}Z(X_k)>\varepsilon\right)\leq(1-p)^K.\] Hence, for \(0<\delta<1\), choosing \[K\geq\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-p)}\right\rceil\] gives an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary selected candidate with probability at least \(1-\delta\). If one run costs \(\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon)\), the total cost is \(K\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon)=O(\mathcal{C}(\varepsilon)\log(1/\delta))\) for fixed \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating a constant-confidence method independently O(log(1/delta)) times and reliably selecting a successful candidate amplifies the success probability to at least 1-delta, with the same logarithmic factor in total cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Monro asymptotic stationarity measured by the Moreau-envelope gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x_t)\) be stochastic iterates for a proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded-below, \(\rho\)-weakly convex function \(f\). Suppose the oracle errors are adapted martingale differences with uniformly bounded conditional second moments, the iterates are almost surely bounded, and the stepsizes satisfy \(\sum_t\alpha_t=\infty\) and \(\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty\). If the method admits the standard conditional envelope-descent inequality for some \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), then \[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_t\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_t)\|^2<\infty\quad\text{almost surely},\] and hence \(\liminf_{t\to\infty}\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_t)\|=0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Robbins–Monro stepsizes, bounded iterates, martingale noise, and envelope descent, the envelope-gradient residual has almost-sure liminf zero.
assumptions_latex: The iterates are almost surely bounded and satisfy a conditional Moreau-envelope descent inequality.
Oracle errors are adapted martingale differences with uniformly bounded conditional second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Almost surely, \(\sum_t\alpha_t\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_t)\|^2<\infty\) and \(\liminf_t\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_t)\|=0\).
review_flags: A stochastic quasi-Fejér or supermartingale theorem and method-specific descent inequality must be cited.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the asymptotic stationarity leaf. The conclusion is plausible under an appropriate almost-supermartingale envelope-descent inequality, but that inequality is not stated precisely, and no locator supports the passage to almost-sure weighted summability. A method-specific source and exact conditional inequality are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Point Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity of accumulation points under vanishing envelope residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, and fix \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\). Suppose a sample path \((x_t)\) is bounded and satisfies \(\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_t)\|\to0\). Every cluster point \(\bar x\) of this path then satisfies \(\nabla f_\lambda(\bar x)=0\). Since \(f_\lambda\) is continuously differentiable and its stationary points coincide with stationary points of \(f\), it follows that \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\). Hence every cluster point is stationary, although the full sequence need not converge without additional geometric assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If bounded iterates have vanishing Moreau-envelope gradient, every cluster point is stationary for the original weakly convex objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
\(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), the sequence is bounded, and \(\|\nabla f_\lambda(x_t)\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every cluster point \(\bar x\) satisfies \(\nabla f_\lambda(\bar x)=0\) and \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: cluster point of the iterate sequence

review_flags: The locator is provisional for Moreau-envelope properties; exact stationary-point equivalence should be checked.

children.title: Tame Geometric Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers convergence settings based on tame objective geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Tame Geometric Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definable weakly convex objectives in an o-minimal geometric structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an o-minimal structure \(\mathcal{S}\) over the real field. A finite-dimensional weakly convex optimization problem lies in a tame geometric regime when the objective's epigraph \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\leq r\}\] and the feasible set, if present, are definable in \(\mathcal{S}\). Definability is preserved by finite sums, compositions under definable data, and partial minimization under the usual properness conditions. Such objectives admit finite definable stratifications and satisfy a Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality locally at points where the function is finite. These geometric properties supply the additional structure commonly used to strengthen subsequential stationarity into trajectory convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tame regime consists of weakly convex problems whose objective epigraph and constraints are definable in an o-minimal structure.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and defined on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
An o-minimal structure \(\mathcal{S}\) over the real field is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime predicate is \(\operatorname{epi}f\) and the feasible set being definable in \(\mathcal{S}\); consequently, finite definable stratifications and local Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequalities are available.
review_flags: An authoritative tame-geometry source is required for the stratification and Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz consequences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the regime leaf, and epigraph definability is a natural regime predicate. However, the closure under partial minimization, existence of suitable finite stratifications, and local Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz conclusion require precise hypotheses and an authoritative tame-geometry source.

children.title: Stratifiable Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers objectives admitting compatible stratified structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratifiable Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objectives admitting a finite smooth stratification compatible with their subdifferential geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is in the stratifiable regime when its graph admits a locally finite Whitney stratification \(\{M_i\}\) such that each \(M_i\) is a smooth manifold, the restriction of the graph projection to each stratum has constant rank, and the induced restriction of \(f\) is smooth. Compatibility with nonsmooth stationarity additionally requires the limiting subdifferential along each active stratum to obey the appropriate normal-space projection relation. Under this predicate, nonsmooth trajectories can be analyzed piecewise on smooth manifolds, while transitions between strata remain governed by the frontier and Whitney conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratifiable objective has a Whitney-stratified graph with smooth behavior on each stratum and subdifferential geometry compatible with stratum normals.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
The graph of \(f\) admits a locally finite smooth partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is stratifiable when the partition satisfies the Whitney, frontier, constant-rank, smooth-restriction, and subdifferential-compatibility conditions.

notation.meaning: smooth stratum of the graph of f

review_flags: Several inequivalent notions of stratifiable function exist; a source is needed to fix the intended subdifferential-compatibility condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the stratifiable-regime leaf, but the candidate combines several potentially inequivalent definitions. In particular, the required Whitney type, the constant-rank projection condition, and the claimed normal-space projection relation are not formulated precisely enough to establish a single standard regime without a source.

children.title: Stratum Identification Behavior
children.top_down_role: Covers asymptotic interaction between iterates and active strata.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(f(x)=|x|\), whose active zero-dimensional stratum is \(M=\{0\}\).
The iteration is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k(\operatorname{sign}(x_k)+\xi_k)\), where each \(\xi_k\) has a conditional density and \(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb{P}(\exists k_0\ \forall k\ge k_0:\ x_k\in M)=0.\] Thus even when a stochastic weakly convex method satisfies \(x_k\to0\) almost surely, convergence to an active stratum does not imply its finite identification. Exact finite identification requires additional structure, such as perturbations eventually tangent to \(M\), an identification-preserving proximal step, or noise that vanishes in the normal directions after finite time.

notation.meaning: Active stratum containing the limit point

review_flags: Exact stochastic identification boundary requires a source specialized to active-manifold or stratifiable stochastic methods.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification may fail despite almost-sure convergence under continuously distributed normal noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\) and let \(M=\{0\}\) be its active stratum at the unique minimizer. Consider \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k(\operatorname{sign}(x_k)+\xi_k)\), with any deterministic \(x_0\ne0\), positive steps \(\alpha_k\), and perturbations \(\xi_k\) having conditional densities given the past. For every fixed \(k\), the conditional probability that \(x_{k+1}=0\) is zero; hence, by countable subadditivity, \(\mathbb{P}(x_k=0\text{ for some }k)=0\). Consequently, even in parameter regimes where \(x_k\to0\) almost surely, the iterates almost surely never identify \(M\) in finite time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous stochastic perturbations can prevent finite active-stratum identification even when the iterates converge almost surely to the stratum.
knowledge_statements.title: Stratum Identification Behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits Stratum Identification Behavior, and the atom-avoidance argument is mathematically plausible when the steps are deterministic and each perturbation has a conditional density given the past. However, no inspectable source supports either this stochastic identification example or the broader claims about structures sufficient for finite identification. A source specialized to stochastic active-manifold or stratifiable identification is required.

children.title: Stochastic Perturbation Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Covers noise regimes compatible with geometric convergence arguments.

assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal{F}_k)\) is the natural filtration and \(e_k=b_k+\xi_k\), with \(b_k=\mathbb{E}[e_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accumulated bias \(\sum_k\alpha_k b_k\) is absolutely convergent, and the martingale series \(\sum_k\alpha_k\xi_k\) converges almost surely and in \(L^2\). Therefore these perturbations contribute only a convergent error to a stochastic approximation recursion and are compatible with standard almost-sure descent and limiting-stationarity arguments.

notation.meaning: Information available before the kth oracle sample

review_flags: A stochastic-approximation source matching the weakly convex stratifiable setting is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A summable-bias, square-summable-variance compatibility condition for asymptotic stochastic arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbation sequence \((e_k)\) is compatible with a diminishing-step stochastic approximation if, relative to a filtration \((\mathcal{F}_k)\), it decomposes as \(e_k=b_k+\xi_k\), where \(b_k=\mathbb{E}[e_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\), \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]=0\), and \(\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_k\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\le\sigma_k^2\) almost surely. For positive steps \((\alpha_k)\), require \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k\|b_k\|<\infty,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2\sigma_k^2<\infty.\] These conditions make the cumulative predictable error summable and the weighted martingale perturbation convergent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatibility holds when weighted bias is summable, weighted conditional variance is square summable, and the steps remain nonsummable.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Perturbation Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the terminal container, but the stated assumptions do not by themselves justify the conclusion that the martingale series converges in L2: an almost-sure bound on the predictable quadratic variation is weaker than an integrable total second-moment bound. The claim that these errors are compatible with descent and limiting-stationarity arguments also depends on the recursion and stability hypotheses. An authoritative stochastic-approximation source is needed to determine and state the correct convergence conditions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Moreau envelope \(f_\lambda\) is continuously differentiable and \[\nabla f_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p).\] Hence \(\|\nabla f_\lambda(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) certifies an \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient of the original convex objective at the nearby point \(p\), with \(\|x-p\|\le\lambda\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Proximal point of f at x with parameter lambda

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The weak-convexity parameter specializes to zero, giving the classical convex Moreau-envelope certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\lambda>0\), define \[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\in\mathop{\arg\min}_{y}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\}.\] The minimizer is unique, the Moreau envelope \(f_\lambda\) is continuously differentiable, and \[\nabla f_\lambda(x)=\frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial f(p).\] Thus envelope stationarity at \(x\) is exactly a convex-subgradient certificate at the associated proximal point \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the convex case, the Moreau-envelope gradient is exactly a subgradient at the proximal point and measures their displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Specialization

children.title: Relative Strong Convexity
children.top_down_role: Covers strong convexity measured relative to a reference geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex and \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to \(h\) precisely when \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\mu D_h(y,x)\] for all admissible \(x,y\) and \(v\in\partial f(x)\), where \(D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\).
review_flags: The supplied locator concerns weak convexity rather than explicitly relative strong convexity; exact source confirmation is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient formulation of relative strong convexity with a differentiable Bregman reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex, let \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and strictly convex, and define \[D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle.\] A proper function \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex relative to \(h\), for \(\mu\ge0\), if for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), every \(v\in\partial f(x)\), and every \(y\in C\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+\mu D_h(y,x).\] For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), this reduces to ordinary \(\mu\)-strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative strong convexity replaces the Euclidean quadratic term by the Bregman divergence generated by a reference function.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Strong Convexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is the correct role for Relative Strong Convexity, but no source is supplied and the formulation does not specify the subdifferential convention or the regularity and domain conditions under which the all-subgradients inequality is equivalent to the intended relative strong-convexity definition. For a merely proper function, the condition can also become vacuous at points with empty subdifferential. A source is required to fix the precise standard formulation.

children.title: Quadratic Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers objective growth away from the solution set.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and has nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\mathop{\arg\min}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic growth on \(U\) is the inequality \[f(x)-f^*\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] The global regime takes \(U=\mathbb{R}^d\); a local regime requires the same inequality only near \(X^*\) or a selected minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local and global Euclidean quadratic-growth regimes are distinguished by the neighborhood.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Convex Quadratic and Nonlinear Programs p. 80

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(f^*=\inf f\), and suppose \(X^*=\mathop{\arg\min}f\ne\varnothing\). The function has quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu>0\) on a set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) if \[f(x)-f^*\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] The regime is global when \(U=\mathbb{R}^d\), and local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\) or of a designated minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth lower-bounds objective error by a positive multiple of squared distance to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Convex Quadratic and Nonlinear Programs p. 80

children.title: Growth-to-Certificate Transfer
children.top_down_role: Covers how growth properties strengthen stationarity interpretation.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and satisfies quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu>0\).
\(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) lies in the growth neighborhood, and \(g=\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Since \(g\in\partial f(p)\), convexity and quadratic growth imply \[\operatorname{dist}(p,X^*)\le\frac{2}{\mu}\|g\|,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\left(\lambda+\frac{2}{\mu}\right)\|g\|.\] Thus the computable envelope residual \(\|g\|=\|\nabla f_\lambda(x)\|\) transfers directly to a distance-to-solution certificate.
review_flags: A source explicitly stating this growth-to-proximal-residual transfer is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex quadratic growth converts a Moreau-envelope residual into a solution-distance certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with minimizer set \(X^*\ne\varnothing\), and suppose \(f(z)-f^*\ge\tfrac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(z,X^*)\) in a neighborhood containing \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). Set \(g=\lambda^{-1}(x-p)\). Since \(g\in\partial f(p)\), convexity gives \(f(p)-f^*\le\|g\|\operatorname{dist}(p,X^*)\). Combining the inequalities yields \[\operatorname{dist}(p,X^*)\le\frac{2}{\mu}\|g\|,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\left(\lambda+\frac{2}{\mu}\right)\|g\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convex quadratic growth, a small proximal residual certifies that both the proximal point and query point are near the solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Growth-to-Certificate Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role exactly fits Growth-to-Certificate Transfer, and the constants follow from convexity, the proximal optimality relation, quadratic growth at the proximal point, and the triangle inequality. Nevertheless, the record provides no citation for this nontrivial transfer result. An inspectable source stating the bound or its constituent theorem is required.

children.title: Local Growth Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Covers improvements valid only near the solution set.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A radius-\(r\) local quadratic-growth neighborhood is \[U_r=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le r\},\] together with the requirement \[f(x)-f^*\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X^*)\quad\text{for all }x\in U_r\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] Any local rate or certificate using this inequality is conditional on the iterates or associated proximal points remaining in \(U_r\).

notation.meaning: Closed radius-r neighborhood of the solution set

review_flags: A source treating invariant local growth neighborhoods for stochastic iterates is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The growth inequality is restricted to a metric neighborhood that must contain the relevant iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, with \(X^*=\mathop{\arg\min}f\ne\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\inf f\). For \(r>0\), define the solution neighborhood \[U_r=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le r\}.\] A local quadratic-growth regime with parameters \((\mu,r)\), where \(\mu>0\), means \[f(x)-f^*\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U_r\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] Conclusions derived from this local inequality apply only while the iterates, proximal points, or comparison points used by the analysis belong to \(U_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local growth holds only within a fixed neighborhood of the solution set, so rate guarantees require the analyzed points to stay there.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Growth Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits Local Growth Neighborhoods, and the radius-based quadratic-growth regime is internally precise. The final limitation is also appropriately conditional rather than claiming invariance. No source is supplied, however, for either this neighborhood convention or its use in stochastic local analyses.

children.title: Sharpness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers objectives with linear growth away from relevant solution sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sharpness regime is \[f(x)-f^*\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] It is global if \(U=\mathbb{R}^d\) and local otherwise. Unlike quadratic growth, the objective gap grows at least linearly with distance from the minimizer set.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the sharpness definition in this stochastic weakly convex context.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear objective growth away from the minimizer set, locally or globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(f^*=\inf f\), and suppose \(X^*=\mathop{\arg\min}f\ne\varnothing\). The function is sharp with modulus \(\mu>0\) on a set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) if \[f(x)-f^*\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] The sharpness regime is global when \(U=\mathbb{R}^d\), and local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\) or of a selected minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharpness requires objective error to grow at least linearly with distance from the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits Sharpness Regimes, and the local/global linear-growth definition is mathematically standard and clearly distinguished from quadratic growth. No source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is provided, so the candidate lacks the required evidence.

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers bounds connecting residual size to solution-set distance.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A linear objective error bound on \(U\) is \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] The condition is global for \(U=\mathbb{R}^d\) and local otherwise. It is a solution-distance certificate expressed through observable objective suboptimality when \(f^*\) is known.
review_flags: The term error bound has several residual-based variants; this record selects the objective-gap version dictated by the sharpness correspondence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap error bound paired with the neighboring sharpness nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(f^*=\inf f\), and suppose \(X^*=\mathop{\arg\min}f\ne\varnothing\). The objective-gap error-bound condition with constant \(\kappa>0\) on \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] It is a global error bound when \(U=\mathbb{R}^d\), and a local error bound when \(U\) is a neighborhood of the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective error bound controls distance to the solution set by a constant times objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is appropriate, and the record explicitly selects the objective-gap error-bound convention relevant to the neighboring sharpness nodes. Because error bound also commonly denotes residual, metric-subregularity, and subgradient formulations, an inspectable source is required to support this exact convention in the intended hierarchy.

children.title: Local Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers settings where sharpness and error bounds imply comparable behavior.

assumptions_latex: Both inequalities are interpreted on the same neighborhood \(U\) of \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local sharpness inequality \[f(x)-f^*\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\] holds on \(U\) if and only if the local objective error bound \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\] holds there, with reciprocal constants \(\kappa=1/\mu\) and \(\mu=1/\kappa\).
review_flags: The equivalence is algebraic for the selected objective-gap error-bound convention; other residual conventions require additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local equivalence for the objective-gap convention, not for arbitrary residual error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(X^*=\mathop{\arg\min}f\ne\varnothing\), and fix a neighborhood \(U\) of \(X^*\). The sharpness inequality \[f(x)-f^*\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f)\] is equivalent to the objective-gap error bound \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f).\] The constants correspond exactly by \(\kappa=1/\mu\), or equivalently \(\mu=1/\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the same neighborhood, sharpness and the objective-gap error bound are the same inequality with reciprocal constants.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality role fits Local Equivalence Regimes. For the explicitly selected objective-gap error bound on the same neighborhood, the two displayed conditions are indeed the same inequality with reciprocal constants. No citation is supplied, however, and the scope must remain distinguished from non-equivalent residual-based error bounds.

children.title: Stochastic Noise Floors
children.top_down_role: Covers limits on geometric improvements imposed by persistent noise.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a closed convex set \(C\), with minimizer \(x^*\).
The projected update is \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\alpha G_k)\), where \(\mathbb{E}[G_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|G_k\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\le G^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mean-square recursion satisfies \[\mathbb{E}\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|^2\le(1-2\alpha\mu)\mathbb{E}\|x_k-x^*\|^2+\alpha^2G^2,\] and therefore \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\|x_k-x^*\|^2\le\frac{\alpha G^2}{2\mu}.\] A constant step thus produces an \(O(\alpha)\) mean-square noise floor rather than exact convergence.
review_flags: The supplied relative-noise locator does not directly certify this absolute second-moment constant-step bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected stochastic subgradient noise floor under strong convexity and a constant step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a closed convex set \(C\), with minimizer \(x^*\), and consider \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\alpha G_k)\). Assume \(\mathbb{E}[G_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\|G_k\|^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\le G^2\), and \(0<\alpha<1/(2\mu)\). Then \[\mathbb{E}\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|^2\le(1-2\alpha\mu)\mathbb{E}\|x_k-x^*\|^2+\alpha^2G^2,\] so \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\|x_k-x^*\|^2\le\frac{\alpha G^2}{2\mu}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a constant step and bounded stochastic subgradient second moment, strong convexity yields an asymptotic mean-square error proportional to the step size.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Noise Floors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A quantitative bound is an appropriate role for Stochastic Noise Floors. Under the stated strong-convexity convention and conditional unbiasedness, the projected recursion and O(alpha) limiting mean-square floor are plausible with the displayed constants. No inspectable source supports this nontrivial stochastic recursion, and the supplied inventory's relative deterministic-noise locator does not match it.

children.title: Finite-Sum Specializations
children.top_down_role: Covers improvements tied to a finite component structure.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is uniformly distributed on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the component oracle returns \(g_I(x)\in\partial f_I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-sum objective and its unbiased component oracle admit the representation \[F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)=\mathbb{E}[f_I(x)],\qquad \mathbb{E}[g_I(x)]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x).\] Whenever the chosen subdifferential sum rule applies, \(n^{-1}\sum_i g_i(x)\in\partial F(x)\), so uniform component sampling supplies an unbiased stochastic subgradient of \(F\).
review_flags: A finite-sum nonsmooth stochastic-method source with the applicable subdifferential sum rule is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform component sampling representation, with subdifferential regularity stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For component functions \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \[F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x).\] If \(I\) is uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then \[F(x)=\mathbb{E}[f_I(x)].\] Given selections \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\) with finite norms, the component oracle satisfies \[\mathbb{E}[g_I(x)]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x).\] If the relevant subdifferential sum rule holds at \(x\), then \(n^{-1}\sum_i g_i(x)\in\partial F(x)\); hence component sampling gives an unbiased stochastic subgradient representation of the finite-sum problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum is an expectation over a uniform component index, and component subgradients form an unbiased oracle when the subdifferential sum rule holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Specializations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits Finite-Sum Specializations. The expectation identities are correct, and the statement appropriately makes the stochastic-subgradient conclusion conditional on an applicable sum rule. Still, the subdifferential type and corresponding sum-rule hypotheses are not fixed, and no finite-sum nonsmooth source is cited to resolve them.

children.title: Mean-Square-Smooth Specializations
children.top_down_role: Covers improvements based on mean-square smooth oracle variation.

assumptions_latex: The objective has finite-sum form \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Each component admits a measurable oracle selection \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The component oracle is mean-square smooth with constant \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum oracle condition for component subgradient selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A component oracle \(g_I\) is mean-square smooth with constant \(L\geq 0\) if, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), the same randomly sampled index is used at both points and
\[
\mathbb{E}_I\!\left[\left\|g_I(x)-g_I(y)\right\|^2\right]\leq L^2\left\|x-y\right\|^2.
\]
For uniform finite-sum sampling, this is equivalently
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left\|g_i(x)-g_i(y)\right\|^2\leq L^2\left\|x-y\right\|^2.
\]
The condition concerns the coupled component oracle and is stronger than smoothness of the averaged objective alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-square smoothness bounds the average squared change of component subgradients, evaluated with the same sampled component, by the squared distance between the query points.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Square-Smooth Specializations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the mean-square-smooth specialization container and condition is the appropriate content kind. The equivalence under uniform sampling is mathematically consistent, but no cited source supports this particular coupled selected-subgradient formulation or clarifies whether the condition is imposed on a fixed measurable selection or on the oracle law. An authoritative source with a specific definition, section, theorem, or page locator is required.

children.title: Variance-Reduction Access
children.top_down_role: Covers oracle structures that support variance-reduced methods.

assumptions_latex: A reference point \(\widetilde x\) and its full averaged oracle value \(\overline g(\widetilde x)=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n g_j(\widetilde x)\) are available.
An index \(I\) is sampled uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimator satisfies \(\mathbb{E}_I[v(x;\widetilde x)]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Snapshot control-variate access for a finite-sum component oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(\widetilde x\), first compute and store
\[
\overline g(\widetilde x)=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n g_j(\widetilde x).
\]
At a current point \(x\), sample \(I\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and return
\[
v(x;\widetilde x)=g_I(x)-g_I(\widetilde x)+\overline g(\widetilde x).
\]
Then \(v(x;\widetilde x)\) is conditionally unbiased for the averaged selected oracle. If the oracle is mean-square smooth with constant \(L\), its conditional variance obeys
\[
\mathbb{E}_I\!\left[\left\|v(x;\widetilde x)-\mathbb{E}_I v(x;\widetilde x)\right\|^2\right]\leq L^2\left\|x-\widetilde x\right\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A snapshot control variate combines one component difference with a stored full average, preserving unbiasedness while making variance shrink near the snapshot.
knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduction Access

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The snapshot estimator and variance calculation fit Variance-Reduction Access, and algorithm is the appropriate content kind. Algebraically, the variance bound follows from the stated mean-square increment condition. However, no source establishes this construction for the selected nonsmooth component oracles used here, and the compatibility of the selections at the current and snapshot points is not sourced.

children.title: Specialization Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Covers limits on carrying specialized rates into general stochastic models.

assumptions_latex: Only unbiasedness and a uniform second-moment bound \(\mathbb{E}\|g_I(x)\|^2\leq G^2\) are assumed.
No coupled mean-square increment bound is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The variance estimate \(\operatorname{Var}(v(x;\widetilde x))\leq L^2\|x-\widetilde x\|^2\) cannot be inferred.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for transferring finite-sum variance-reduced rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bounded second moment does not imply distance-sensitive control of component increments. Indeed, let \(I\) be Rademacher, let \(g_I(0)=I\), and set \(g_I(x)=-I\) for every \(x\neq 0\). Then \(\mathbb{E}[g_I(x)]=0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[|g_I(x)|^2]=1\) for all \(x\), but for every \(x\neq0\),
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[|g_I(x)-g_I(0)|^2\right]=4.
\]
Consequently no finite \(L\) yields a bound by \(L^2|x|^2\) near zero. Thus a rate relying on snapshot variance decay cannot be transferred from mean-square-smooth access using bounded variance alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded oracle variance alone does not make component differences shrink with distance, so mean-square-smooth variance-reduction rates do not automatically transfer.
knowledge_statements.title: Specialization Transfer Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct mathematical role for this leaf, and the example does show that bounded second moments alone do not imply a mean-square increment bound for an abstract unbiased oracle. In the local stochastic weakly convex subgradient context, however, the record does not show that the discontinuous oracle is an admissible subgradient selection of the stipulated component functions. A source or an admissible weakly convex counterexample is needed before the claimed specialization-transfer boundary is reliable in this container.

children.title: Sample Complexity
children.top_down_role: Covers the number of stochastic samples required for a target certificate.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm returns an output \(X\) after adaptively requesting independent data samples.
Accuracy is measured by \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F_\lambda(X)\|\leq\varepsilon\), where \(F_\lambda\) is a differentiable Moreau envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sample complexity is the least \(N\) guaranteeing the stated envelope-stationarity criterion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition under expected Moreau-envelope stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a specified problem class and sampling oracle, define the sample complexity
\[
N_{\mathrm{samp}}(\varepsilon)=\inf\left\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\text{an admissible algorithm using at most \(N\) sample draws returns \(X\) with \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F_\lambda(X)\|\leq\varepsilon\)}\right\}.
\]
A draw is charged whenever a previously unavailable random datum is obtained. Repeated evaluations on an already stored datum do not increase \(N_{\mathrm{samp}}\), although they may increase oracle work. If no admissible algorithm attains the criterion, the infimum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample complexity counts distinct random data draws needed to produce an iterate whose expected Moreau-envelope gradient norm is at most the target tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement defines a sample-complexity accounting convention rather than giving a complexity bound, so definition would be the appropriate content kind. The convention that repeated work on stored data is free in sample count is not universal and requires a source and a precisely specified oracle model. The displayed set also embeds \(\cdot\) delimiters inside \(\text{...}\) while already in display math and should be normalized when the sourced convention is revised.

children.title: Subgradient-Evaluation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Covers the number of subgradient oracle evaluations required.

assumptions_latex: Each component-oracle call returns one selected stochastic or finite-sum subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Subgradient-evaluation complexity is the least number of charged component-oracle evaluations attaining the criterion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-subgradient work under envelope stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed component-oracle model, define
\[
N_{\mathrm{sub}}(\varepsilon)=\inf\left\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\text{an admissible algorithm making at most \(N\) component-subgradient evaluations returns \(X\) with \(\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F_\lambda(X)\|\leq\varepsilon\)}\right\}.
\]
Every evaluation of \(g_i(x)\) is charged, including repeated evaluations using the same stored sample or component index. Hence \(N_{\mathrm{sub}}\) measures computational oracle work and need not equal the number of distinct samples drawn.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradient-evaluation complexity counts every component subgradient computation, including repeated work on stored samples, needed to reach envelope stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient-Evaluation Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a definition of an evaluation-count convention, not a stated asymptotic or finite complexity bound; definition is the appropriate content kind. Counting every repeated component evaluation is coherent but must be tied to an authoritative oracle model. No citation is supplied, and the display contains nested math delimiters inside \(\text{...}\), which should be repaired in a sourced replacement.

children.title: Sample-Reuse Accounting
children.top_down_role: Covers complexity accounting when samples support multiple evaluations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run has sample cost \(S\) and subgradient-evaluation cost \(\sum_{j=1}^S r_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting identity separating data acquisition from repeated oracle work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a run obtains \(S\) distinct data samples and evaluates the sample oracle on stored sample \(j\) exactly \(r_j\) times. Under distinct-draw accounting and per-evaluation oracle accounting,
\[
N_{\mathrm{samp}}=S,
\qquad
N_{\mathrm{sub}}=Q=\sum_{j=1}^{S}r_j.
\]
Therefore \(N_{\mathrm{samp}}\leq N_{\mathrm{sub}}\), with equality exactly when \(r_j=1\) for every sampled datum. Reusing samples can reduce acquisition cost relative to oracle work, but it does not make repeated component computations free.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If stored sample j is queried r_j times, sample cost is the number of distinct samples while oracle work is the sum of all reuse counts.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Reuse Accounting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is an appropriate content kind, and the identity is correct under the explicitly stated distinct-draw and per-evaluation accounting conventions. Those conventions are model-dependent, however, and no source is supplied. In particular, the meaning of a distinct sample and whether storage or replay is permitted must be grounded in a cited oracle model.

children.title: Batching Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Covers changes in sample and evaluation costs caused by batching.

assumptions_latex: The vectors \(G_1,\ldots,G_b\) are conditionally independent with common conditional mean \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A batch of size \(b\) costs \(b\) evaluations and has conditional mean-square error at most \(\sigma^2/b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent minibatch variance-work tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the minibatch estimator
\[
\overline G_b=\frac1b\sum_{j=1}^b G_j.
\]
Conditional independence and centering give
\[
\mathbb{E}[\overline G_b\mid\mathcal F]=g,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\|\overline G_b-g\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
=\frac1{b^2}\sum_{j=1}^b\mathbb{E}[\|G_j-g\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
\leq\frac{\sigma^2}{b}.
\]
Thus the standard deviation falls as \(b^{-1/2}\), while serial sample and oracle work grow linearly as \(b\). Without independence, the covariance terms must also be charged and the \(1/b\) reduction need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch of b independent oracle calls multiplies serial work by b while reducing the estimator's mean-square error by a factor of b.
knowledge_statements.title: Batching Cost Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional mean and mean-square calculation are correct for conditionally independent, square-integrable vector observations with common conditional mean, and property fits the leaf. The work-versus-variance interpretation nevertheless has no cited support in the relevant stochastic-oracle setting. A specific authoritative locator is required, including the independence and per-call charging convention.

assumptions_latex: At each query point \(x\), a model oracle returns a random function \(m_x(\cdot;\xi)\).
The model satisfies the accuracy and one-sided approximation conditions specified by the problem class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model-oracle complexity is the least number of model constructions needed to attain the prescribed output criterion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-count convention for stochastic local-model methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a class of admissible stochastic models and an output criterion \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\). A model-oracle call at \(x\) draws \(\xi\) and returns a representation of \(m_x(\cdot;\xi)\); solving or approximately minimizing that returned model is accounted for separately. The model-oracle complexity is
\[
N_{\mathrm{mod}}(\varepsilon)=\inf\left\{N\in\mathbb N:\text{an admissible algorithm using at most \(N\) model-oracle calls returns \(X\) satisfying \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\)}\right\}.
\]
For envelope stationarity one may take \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\) to mean \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F_\lambda(X)\|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model-oracle complexity counts stochastic local models constructed to reach a stated accuracy, while the work used to solve each returned model is tracked separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Oracle Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines model-oracle complexity rather than supplying a complexity bound, so definition is the appropriate content kind. More importantly, the admissible model class, representation returned by a call, and output criterion are placeholders, making the quantity dependent on unspecified conventions. No source resolves those conventions. The displayed set also uses nested math delimiters within \(\text{...}\) and should be normalized in a sourced revision.

assumptions_latex: Each subproblem is returned with a prescribed exact or inexact solution certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proximal-subproblem complexity is the number of certified subproblem solves required to meet the outer accuracy criterion.

notation.meaning: local model at outer iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer complexity counted in certified proximal model solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At outer iteration \(k\), one proximal subproblem is
\[
\min_{y\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{m_k(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda_k}\|y-x_k\|^2\right\}.
\]
Fix an admissible certificate defining when this problem is solved, and fix an outer criterion \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\). Then
\[
N_{\mathrm{prox}}(\varepsilon)=\inf\left\{K\in\mathbb N:\text{an admissible method using at most \(K\) certified proximal solves returns \(X\) satisfying \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\)}\right\}.
\]
This count treats each certified solve as one unit; inner model, subgradient, or arithmetic work must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal-subproblem complexity counts certified regularized model solves needed for outer accuracy; it does not by itself measure the inner work of each solve.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Subproblem Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This record defines an outer accounting unit rather than stating a complexity bound; definition is the appropriate content kind. The value of the count depends essentially on the exact or inexact subproblem certificate, which is left as an unspecified admissible certificate, and no source fixes that convention. The displayed infimum also contains nested math delimiters inside \(\text{...}\), requiring cleanup in a sourced revision.

assumptions_latex: The oracle returns only noisy function values \(Y(x,\xi)\), not derivatives.
The algorithm must return \(X\) satisfying a fixed stationarity criterion \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zeroth-order query complexity is the least number of charged function-value observations attaining \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-value query count for derivative-free envelope stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A zeroth-order query is one requested scalar observation \(Y(x,xi)\) at a chosen point \(x\). For a specified noise model and admissible algorithm class, define
\[
N_0(\varepsilon)=\inf\left\{N\in\mathbb N:\text{an algorithm using at most \(N\) scalar observations returns \(X\) satisfying \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon(X)\)}\right\}.
\]
If a gradient estimator uses \(q\) function values per realization and the method constructs \(T\) such estimators, then its query work is \(qT\). Shared randomness changes the estimator's variance but does not reduce the number of scalar observations charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeroth-order complexity counts scalar function observations. An estimator using q values on each of T occasions incurs qT queries, regardless of shared randomness.
knowledge_statements.title: Zeroth-Order Query Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record is a definition of query complexity, not a complexity bound, so definition is the appropriate content kind. In the first sentence of statement_latex, \(Y(x,xi)\) uses the undefined product-like token xi instead of the declared random variable \(\xi\). The scalar-observation and shared-randomness charging conventions are also source-dependent and unsupported. Nested delimiters inside the displayed \(\text{...}\) expression should be removed in the sourced correction.

children.title: Minibatch Work Complexity
children.top_down_role: Covers total work as a function of minibatch size.

assumptions_latex: Iteration \(t\) forms a minibatch containing \(b_t\) oracle evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total minibatch oracle work is \(W=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total oracle work for variable-size minibatches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If iteration \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\) evaluates \(b_t\) sample or component oracles, its serial-equivalent oracle work is \(b_t\), and the complete run has
\[
W=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t.
\]
For a constant batch size \(b\), this becomes \(W=bT\). Concurrent execution can reduce elapsed depth but does not reduce \(W\). If an iteration additionally computes a full finite-sum reference value using \(n\) components, that refresh contributes another \(n\) units of work and must be included in the sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minibatch work is the sum of all batch sizes, including full finite-sum refreshes; parallel execution changes elapsed depth but not total oracle work.
knowledge_statements.title: Minibatch Work Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a work-accounting identity, not a bound on the work required to attain a specified accuracy; property is the better content kind for this exact statement. The identity is correct under unit-cost component-oracle accounting, including the separately mentioned full refreshes, but no authoritative source fixes that cost model.

children.title: Parallel Depth Complexity
children.top_down_role: Covers sequential depth under concurrent oracle evaluation.

assumptions_latex: At most \(p\) oracle evaluations can be executed concurrently in one round.
Iteration \(t\) requires a batch of \(b_t\) evaluations before the next iteration begins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle-round depth is \(D_p=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\lceil b_t/p\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous oracle depth with bounded processor count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under synchronous execution with \(p\geq1\) identical processors, a batch of \(b_t\) independent oracle calls occupies \(\lceil b_t/p\rceil\) oracle rounds. When iterations are sequentially dependent, the complete run therefore has depth
\[
D_p=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\left\lceil\frac{b_t}{p}\right\rceil.
\]
Writing \(W=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}b_t\), one has
\[
\max\{T,\lceil W/p\rceil\}\leq D_p\leq W.
\]
This idealized depth excludes communication, synchronization, and aggregation latency; those costs require a separate parallel machine model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With p processors and sequentially dependent iterations, each batch needs ceiling(b_t/p) oracle rounds, so total idealized depth is their sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Depth Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The depth formula and its inequalities are correct under the stated synchronous, sequential-iteration, unit-time oracle model. The record is principally a parallel-depth representation/property rather than a complexity bound establishing the resources needed for an accuracy target. No source supports the chosen machine model or accounting convention, so a cited definition with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Processor Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers useful speedup as computational resources increase.

knowledge_statements.title: Processor Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies efficient and saturated processor counts through a prescribed parallel-efficiency threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the admissible processor counts, with \(1\in\mathcal P\), and let \(T_P(\varepsilon)>0\) be the wall-clock time required by a fixed stochastic algorithm to reach accuracy \(\varepsilon\) using \(P\in\mathcal P\) identical processors. Define \(S_P(\varepsilon)=T_1(\varepsilon)/T_P(\varepsilon)\) and \(E_P(\varepsilon)=S_P(\varepsilon)/P\). For \(\eta\in(0,1)\), the \(\eta\)-efficient set is \(\mathcal P_\eta(\varepsilon)=\{P\in\mathcal P:E_P(\varepsilon)\geq\eta\}\), and its scaling boundary is \(P_\eta(\varepsilon)=\sup\mathcal P_\eta(\varepsilon)\) in \([1,+\infty]\). An admissible count is \(\eta\)-efficient when it belongs to \(\mathcal P_\eta(\varepsilon)\), and it is beyond the \(\eta\)-efficiency boundary when \(P>P_\eta(\varepsilon)\). If \(P_\eta(\varepsilon)\in\mathcal P_\eta(\varepsilon)\), then it is the largest \(\eta\)-efficient processor count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Speedup and efficiency are measured relative to one processor. A threshold defines the efficient processor set and its supremal scaling boundary, which is a largest efficient count only when attained.
assumptions_latex: All processor counts use the same algorithm, accuracy criterion, and hardware model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_P(\varepsilon)\geq\eta\iff T_P(\varepsilon)\leq T_1(\varepsilon)/(\eta P)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this parallel-complexity convention.

children.title: Communication-Limited Scaling
children.top_down_role: Covers parallel regimes dominated by coordination or data movement.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Limited Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when communication latency prevents further minibatch-parallel speedup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one outer iteration performs divisible work \(W>0\), requires \(R\geq1\) synchronization rounds, and has nonparallel overhead \(S\geq0\). Under the time model \(T_P=W/P+R\ell(P)+S\), where \(\ell(P)\) is the latency per round, computation ceases to dominate once \(W/P\leq R\ell(P)+S\). In that communication-limited regime, increasing \(P\) can remove at most the term \(W/P\); hence \(T_P\geq R\ell(P)+S\), and speedup is bounded by \(T_1/(R\ell(P)+S)\). If \(\ell(P)\) is nondecreasing, communication time cannot be reduced by adding processors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling saturates when synchronized communication and serial overhead equal or exceed the remaining divisible computation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W/P\leq R\ell(P)+S\Longrightarrow T_P\geq R\ell(P)+S\).
review_flags: The supplied inventory contains no parallel communication model source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the deductions follow from the stated timing model, but no cited source supports that communication model or its interpretation.

children.title: Complexity Comparison Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Uses neighboring complexity theories as benchmarks without claiming a chapter-specific lower-bound theory that the inspected sources do not support.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares envelope stationarity with gradient stationarity in the smooth subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and choose \(0<\lambda<1/L\). For \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\), the Moreau envelope satisfies \(
abla f_\lambda(x)=(x-y)/\lambda\). First-order optimality of the proximal subproblem gives \((x-y)/\lambda=
abla f(y)\), and therefore \(\|
abla f_\lambda(x)\|=\|
abla f(y)\|\). Moreover, Lipschitz continuity yields \(\|
abla f(x)\|\leq(1+L\lambda)\|
abla f_\lambda(x)\|\). Thus envelope stationarity implies ordinary smooth stationarity at both the proximal point and, up to a fixed factor, the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth objectives, the envelope gradient equals the ordinary gradient at the proximal point and controls the gradient at the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(
abla f_\lambda(x)=
abla f(y)\quad	ext{and}\quad\|
abla f(x)\|\leq(1+L\lambda)\|
abla f_\lambda(x)\|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Nonsmooth Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates Moreau-envelope stationarity to convex subgradient stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\), the envelope is differentiable and \(
abla f_\lambda(x)=(x-y)/\lambda\in\partial f(y)\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(y))\leq\|
abla f_\lambda(x)\|\), while convexity gives \(f(y)-\inf f\leq\langle
abla f_\lambda(x),y-x^\starangle\) for every minimizer \(x^\star\). Envelope stationarity therefore supplies a subgradient certificate at the nearby proximal point, unlike a subgradient arbitrarily selected at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex nonsmooth objectives, the envelope gradient is a genuine subgradient at the proximal point and certifies its near-stationarity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f_\lambda(x)\in\partial f(y)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(y))\leq\|\nabla f_\lambda(x)\|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Exploitation Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares methods using total primitive-operation cost rather than oracle counts alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an accuracy target \(\varepsilon>0\), let method \(M\) use \(N_i(M,\varepsilon)\) calls to primitive \(i\), each costing \(c_i>0\), and define \(W(M,\varepsilon)=\sum_i c_iN_i(M,\varepsilon)\). A structure-exploiting method \(M_s\) improves upon a generic method \(M_g\) precisely when \(W(M_s,\varepsilon)<W(M_g,\varepsilon)\) under the same accuracy criterion. Thus a smaller stochastic-oracle count alone is insufficient: closed-form proximal mappings, sparsity, separability, or fast linear algebra may reduce particular \(c_i\), whereas expensive structured subproblems may reverse the comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structure is beneficial only when savings in primitive calls and their costs reduce total work under the same accuracy requirement.
assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same accuracy event and computational cost model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_s\text{ is work-superior to }M_g\iff\sum_i c_iN_i(M_s,\varepsilon)<\sum_i c_iN_i(M_g,\varepsilon)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Form Proximal Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies exact evaluation of a proximal mapping when an explicit formula is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(g:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a center \(x\), and \(\lambda>0\), evaluate an available explicit expression \(P_g(x,\lambda)\) and return \(y=P_g(x,\lambda)\). The expression is a valid closed-form proximal mapping when \(y\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z}\{g(z)+\|z-x\|^2/(2\lambda)\}\). If \(g\) is convex, validity is equivalently certified by \((x-y)/\lambda\in\partial g(y)\); strict convexity of the quadratic then makes the output unique. The algorithm terminates after the finite primitive operations required to evaluate \(P_g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the explicit proximal formula and certify it by the proximal optimality inclusion; convexity guarantees uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Strongly Convex Subproblem Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a linear inner-solve rate for composite strongly convex proximal subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=h+g\), where \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, while \(g:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex. Starting from \(z_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\), apply \(z_{j+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g/L}(z_j-\nabla h(z_j)/L)\). If \(z^\star\) minimizes \(Q\), then \(Q(z_j)-Q(z^\star)\leq(1-\mu/L)^j[Q(z_0)-Q(z^\star)]\). Consequently, for \(0<\delta<Q(z_0)-Q(z^\star)\), running at most \(\left\lceil(L/\mu)\log((Q(z_0)-Q(z^\star))/\delta)\right\rceil\) iterations suffices to obtain objective error at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal gradient solves a smooth-plus-convex strongly convex subproblem to any positive objective tolerance below the initial gap in logarithmically many inner iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{inner}}(\delta)\leq\left\lceil\frac{L}{\mu}\log\frac{Q(z_0)-Q(z^\star)}{\delta}\right\rceil\).

knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth-Newton Subproblem Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a generalized Newton iteration and its local superlinear convergence conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) be locally Lipschitz, and fix a residual tolerance \(\tau\geq0\). To solve \(F(z)=0\), initialize \(z_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\). At iteration \(j\), if \(\|F(z_j)\|\leq\tau\), stop; otherwise choose \(V_j\in\partial_C F(z_j)\), solve \(V_jd_j=-F(z_j)\), and set \(z_{j+1}=z_j+d_j\). If \(F\) is semismooth at a solution \(z^\star\), every matrix in \(\partial_C F(z^\star)\) is nonsingular, and \(z_0\) is sufficiently close to \(z^\star\), then the iteration is well defined locally and \(\|z_{j+1}-z^\star\|=o(\|z_j-z^\star\|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square locally Lipschitz residual map, choose a Clarke generalized Jacobian and solve its Newton system. Semismoothness and generalized-Jacobian regularity yield local superlinear convergence from a sufficiently close initial point.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is locally Lipschitz and semismooth at \(z^\star\).
\(z_0\) lies in the local convergence neighborhood and \(\tau\geq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initializes successive proximal subproblems from the preceding approximate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be \(\rho\)-weakly convex and choose \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\). For successive centers \(x_k\), let \(z_k^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x_k)\). Solve the first proximal subproblem from an arbitrary \(z_{0,0}\); for \(k\geq1\), initialize its inner solver at the preceding returned point, \(z_{k,0}=\widehat z_{k-1}\), and terminate at the prescribed inner tolerance. Since the proximal mapping is \((1-\lambda\rho)^{-1}\)-Lipschitz, exact consecutive solutions satisfy \(\|z_k^\star-z_{k-1}^\star\|\leq\|x_k-x_{k-1}\|/(1-\lambda\rho)\), quantifying when the warm start is close.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize each proximal subproblem with the preceding solution; slowly changing centers make this initialization provably close to the new exact solution.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{k,0}=\widehat z_{k-1}\quad\text{and}\quad\|z_k^\star-z_{k-1}^\star\|\leq\frac{\|x_k-x_{k-1}\|}{1-\lambda\rho}\).
